citations.quote:
Let $n\ge1$ and $A:=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$. For $n\ge2$, define the **normalized type-A Hecke algebra** $H_v(n)$ to be the associative unital $A$-algebra presented by generators $H_{s_1},\ldots,H_{s_{n-1}}$ with relations
$$H_{s_i}^2=1+(v^{-1}-v)H_{s_i},\qquad H_{s_i}H_{s_{i+1}}H_{s_i}=H_{s_{i+1}}H_{s_i}H_{s_{i+1}},\qquad H_{s_i}H_{s_j}=H_{s_j}H_{s_i}\quad(|i-j|>1).$$
For $n=1$, set $H_v(1):=A$.

Here $S_n=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\ldots,n\})$, $s_i=(i\ i+1)$, and $\ell$ is inversion length as in [[def-symmetric-group]] and [[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]. For $w\in S_n$, let $T_w$ be the standard basis element of the generic Hecke algebra of [[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]], formed from any reduced expression of $w$, and after the coefficient specialization $q\mapsto v^{-2}$ put $H_w:=v^{\ell(w)}T_w$. Equivalently, $H_w=H_{s_{i_1}}\cdots H_{s_{i_k}}$ for a reduced expression $w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k}$. The standard-basis theorem [[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]] and rescaling by units show that $\{H_w:w\in S_n\}$ is an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$.

Right multiplication by a generator is
$$H_wH_{s_i}=H_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)+1,\qquad H_wH_{s_i}=H_{ws_i}+(v^{-1}-v)H_w\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)-1.$$

**Dictionary with the generic normalization.** If the generic parameter in [[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]] is denoted by $q$, its relation is $T_i^2=(q-1)T_i+q$. The coefficient map $q\mapsto v^{-2}$ is the stated specialization, and $H_{s_i}=vT_i$. This gives $H_{s_i}^2=1+(v^{-1}-v)H_{s_i}$; the braid and commutation relations are unchanged. The two multiplication cases above are the standard-basis rule after the same rescaling.

**Bar assignment.** Let $F$ be the free associative $\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$-algebra on the generator symbols. Define the semilinear algebra map $\iota_0:F\to F$ by $\iota_0(v)=v^{-1}$ and $\iota_0(H_{s_i})=H_{s_i}-(v^{-1}-v)$. In the quotient $H_v(n)$, the quadratic relation makes this latter element the two-sided inverse $H_{s_i}^{-1}$. The next lemma proves that $\iota_0$ preserves the defining ideal and descends to a well-defined involution $\iota$ on $H_v(n)$.

All items on this page use this normalization. It agrees with Elias–Williamson §3.2 under $H_x=v^{\ell(x)}T_x$ and $q=v^{-2}$.

The presented normalized Hecke algebra $H_v(n)$ has an involutive $A$-linear anti-automorphism $\flat$ defined by $\flat(H_{s_i})=H_{s_i}$. It satisfies $\flat(H_w)=H_{w^{-1}}$ for every $w\in S_n$ and commutes with the bar involution: $\flat\circ\iota=\iota\circ\flat$.

For each $w\in S_n$ there is a unique element $\underline H_w\in H_v(n)$ with (i) $\overline{\underline H_w}=\underline H_w$ and (ii) $\underline H_w\in H_w+\sum_{y<w}v\mathbb Z[v]\,H_y$ (the sum over the lower Bruhat ideal of $w$). The elements $\{\underline H_w\}_{w\in S_n}$ form an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$, and writing $\underline H_w=\sum_{y\le w}p_{y,w}H_y$ one has $p_{w,w}=1$, $p_{y,w}=0$ unless $y\le w$, $p_{y,w}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ for $y<w$, the bar-duality $p_{x,w}=\sum_{y}r_{x,y}\,\overline{p_{y,w}}$ (matrix form $P=R\bar P$), and the symmetry $p_{y^{-1},w^{-1}}=p_{y,w}$. Moreover for $y<w$, with $d=\ell(w)-\ell(y)$: $p_{y,w}=v^{d}+\text{terms of strictly smaller degree}$ and $p_{y,w}\in v^{d}\,\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$; every $p_{y,w}$ has integer coefficients and fixed parity $d\bmod 2$.

For $n\ge1$, let $r_{y,w}\in A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ be the $R$-coefficients of [[def-bruhat-interval-and-r-polynomials]]. (a) **Recursion.** Let $w\in S_n$ and let $s=s_i$ be a simple reflection with $sw<w$. Then for every $y\in S_n$ $$r_{y,w}=r_{sy,sw}\quad\text{if }sy<y,\qquad r_{y,w}=r_{sy,sw}+(v-v^{-1})\,r_{y,sw}\quad\text{if }sy>y .$$ (b) **Support.** $r_{y,w}\ne0$ implies $y\le w$, and $r_{w,w}=1$. (c) **Degree and parity.** For $y\le w$, with $d=\ell(w)-\ell(y)$: $r_{y,w}\in v^{-d}\,\mathbb Z[v^{2},v^{-2}]$; the term of least $v$-degree is $\mathrm{sgn}(y)\,\mathrm{sgn}(w)\,v^{-d}$, and the term of largest $v$-degree is $v^{d}$. (d) **Symmetry.** $\overline{r_{y,w}}=\mathrm{sgn}(y)\mathrm{sgn}(w)r_{y,w}$ and $r_{y^{-1},w^{-1}}=r_{y,w}$. (e) **Matrix inversion.** $\sum_{y\in S_n} r_{x,y}\,\overline{r_{y,z}}=\delta_{x,z}$ for all $x,z$; equivalently the triangular matrices $R=(r_{x,y})$, $\bar R$ satisfy $R\bar R=\bar RR=1$. Here $\mathrm{sgn}(y)=(-1)^{\ell(y)}$ and all coefficients are kept in the variable $v$ of this page.

Identify $\mathbb Z[q]$ with $\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$ by $q\mapsto v^{-2}$. For $y\le w$ in $S_n$, put $d=\ell(w)-\ell(y)$ and define the **Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomial** $P_{y,w}(q)\in\mathbb Z[q]$ by $$P_{y,w}(v^{-2})=v^{-d}p_{y,w},$$ where $\underline H_w=\sum_{y\le w}p_{y,w}H_y$ is the Kazhdan–Lusztig basis of [[lem-type-a-kazhdan-lusztig-basis-has-elementary-triangular-bar-properties]]. The parity clause of that theorem makes the right side a polynomial in $v^{-2}$. The conventions are: $P_{y,w}=0$ unless $y\le w$, $P_{w,w}=1$, $P_{y,w}$ has constant term 1, and for $y<w$ its degree is at most $(\ell(w)-\ell(y)-1)/2$. The **$\mu$-coefficient** is $$\mu(y,w):=	ext{coefficient of }q^{(\ell(w)-\ell(y)-1)/2}	ext{ in }P_{y,w},$$ defined to be 0 when $\ell(w)-\ell(y)$ is even; equivalently $\mu(y,w)$ is the coefficient of $v$ in $p_{y,w}$. One writes $\mu(y|w)
e0$ when $y
e w$ and ($y<w$ and $\mu(y,w)
e0$) or ($w<y$ and $\mu(w,y)
e0$). The dictionary with the literature is recorded for use: with the classical parameter $T_s^2=(q-1)T_s+q$ one has $H_w=v^{\ell(w)}T_w$, the element $\underline H_w$ is the basis element $C'_w$ of [EW], and $h_{y,w}=p_{y,w}$ with $v^{\ell(w)-\ell(y)}P_{y,w}(v^{-2})=h_{y,w}$ [EW, Remark 3.2].

derivations.claim: **Well-definedness and bilinearity (1), (2).** Since $\{H_w\}$ is an $A$-basis by [F1], prescribing $\varepsilon(H_w)=\delta_{e,w}$ and extending $A$-linearly is well defined and unique; the reversal map $a$ is a well-defined $A$-linear anti-automorphism by [F2], and multiplication is $A$-bilinear, so $(h,h')=\varepsilon(a(h)h')$ is a well-defined $A$-bilinear form, for $(ph,qh')=\varepsilon(p\,a(h)\,q\,h')=pq\,\varepsilon(a(h)h')$ with $p,q\in A$. This proves (1) and (2).

**The key identity: base case and recursion.** We prove by induction on $\ell(u)$ that $\varepsilon(H_uH_y)=\delta_{u,y^{-1}}$ for all $u,y\in S_n$; for $u=e$ this reads $H_eH_y=H_y$ and $\varepsilon(H_y)=\delta_{e,y}=\delta_{u,y^{-1}}$, and for $u\ne e$ we choose a simple reflection $s$ with $\ell(us)=\ell(u)-1$ and note that [F1] applied to $w=us$ gives $H_{us}H_s=H_u$, since $(us)s=u$ has length $\ell(u)=\ell(us)+1$.

**The left multiplication rule.** Applying the anti-automorphism $a$ of [F2] to the two cases of [F1] and using $a(H_wH_s)=a(H_s)a(H_w)=H_sH_{w^{-1}}$ and $(ws)^{-1}=sw^{-1}$ gives $H_sH_w=H_{sw}$ if $\ell(sw)=\ell(w)+1$, and $H_sH_w=H_{sw}+(v^{-1}-v)H_w$ if $\ell(sw)<\ell(w)$; this is the rule used in the two cases below.

**The ascent case.** Keep $u\ne e$ and its right descent $s$ from step 2.1, and let $y\in S_n$ satisfy $\ell(sy)>\ell(y)$. Then $H_sH_y=H_{sy}$ by step 3.1, so $\varepsilon(H_uH_y)=\varepsilon(H_{us}H_sH_y)=\varepsilon(H_{us}H_{sy})$; the induction hypothesis applies to the pair $(us,sy)$, whose first length is $\ell(u)-1$, giving $\varepsilon(H_{us}H_{sy})=\delta_{us,(sy)^{-1}}=\delta_{us,y^{-1}s}$, and $us=y^{-1}s$ holds if and only if $u=y^{-1}$ (multiply on the right by $s$ and use $s^2=e$), so $\varepsilon(H_uH_y)=\delta_{u,y^{-1}}$.

**The descent case.** Keep $u,s$ as above and let $\ell(sy)<\ell(y)$. Then $H_sH_y=H_{sy}+(v^{-1}-v)H_y$ by step 3.1, so $\varepsilon(H_uH_y)=\varepsilon(H_{us}H_{sy})+(v^{-1}-v)\varepsilon(H_{us}H_y)$; the induction hypothesis gives $\varepsilon(H_{us}H_{sy})=\delta_{us,y^{-1}s}$ and $\varepsilon(H_{us}H_y)=\delta_{us,y^{-1}}$. If $us=y^{-1}$, then $y=(us)^{-1}=su^{-1}$ and, since $us$ is a right descent of $u$, taking inverses gives $\ell(y)=\ell(su^{-1})=\ell(us)=\ell(u)-1$, while $\ell(sy)=\ell(u^{-1})=\ell(u)>\ell(y)$, contradicting $\ell(sy)<\ell(y)$; hence $\delta_{us,y^{-1}}=0$ and $\varepsilon(H_uH_y)=\delta_{us,y^{-1}s}=\delta_{u,y^{-1}}$.

**The induction concludes.** For every $u\ne e$ the cases $\ell(sy)>\ell(y)$ and $\ell(sy)<\ell(y)$ exhaust all $y$ for the chosen right descent $s$, and each case reduced the first argument's length; with the base case this proves $\varepsilon(H_uH_y)=\delta_{u,y^{-1}}$ for all $u,y\in S_n$.

**Standard orthonormality (4).** For all $x,y$, using $a(H_x)=H_{x^{-1}}$ from [F2] and step 6.1 with $u=x^{-1}$, we get $(H_x,H_y)=\varepsilon(a(H_x)H_y)=\varepsilon(H_{x^{-1}}H_y)=\delta_{x^{-1},y^{-1}}=\delta_{x,y}$, the last equality being injectivity of $w\mapsto w^{-1}$; this proves (4).

**The generator trace identity.** By step 6.1, for every $w$ and simple reflection $s$ one has $\varepsilon(H_wH_s)=\delta_{w,s^{-1}}=\delta_{w,s}$ and $\varepsilon(H_sH_w)=\delta_{s,w^{-1}}=\delta_{w,s}$. Extending over the standard basis gives $\varepsilon(zH_s)=\varepsilon(H_sz)$ for every $z\in H$. In particular the common value for $w=s$ is $1$.

**$\varepsilon$ is a trace and yields the adjunctions (3).** Every element of $H$ is a finite $A$-linear combination of words in the generators, and moving each letter of a word for the second factor to the front one at a time with step 7.2 and bilinearity shows $\varepsilon(xy)=\varepsilon(yx)$ for all $x,y\in H$; consequently, for simple $s$ and $h,h'\in H$, using $a(H_s)=H_s$ from [F2], $(hH_s,h')=\varepsilon(a(hH_s)h')=\varepsilon(H_sa(h)h')=\varepsilon(a(h)h'H_s)=(h,h'H_s)$ and $(H_sh,h')=\varepsilon(a(h)a(H_s)h')=\varepsilon(a(h)H_sh')=(h,H_sh')$, which proves (3) and shows both left and right multiplication by $H_s$ are self-adjoint for $(-,-)$.

**Values on the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis (5).** Write $\underline H_x=\sum_{u\le x}h_{u,x}H_u$ with $h_{u,x}=p_{u,x}\in\mathbb Z[v]$, $h_{x,x}=1$ and $h_{u,x}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ for $u<x$, all other coefficients zero, as in [F3]; then bilinearity (2) and orthonormality from step 7.1 give $(\underline H_x,\underline H_y)=\sum_uh_{u,x}h_{u,y}$. A nonzero term requires $u\le x$ and $u\le y$; if $x
e y$, every surviving term has a factor in $v\mathbb Z[v]$, because $u<x$ or $u<y$ is [F3], and $u=x
e y$ gives $h_{x,y}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ when $x<y$ and $h_{x,y}=0$ otherwise, symmetrically for $u=y$; hence $(\underline H_x,\underline H_y)\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ for $x
e y$. For $x=y$ the term $u=x$ contributes $h_{x,x}^2=1$ and every other term has $u<x$ and contributes to $v^2\mathbb Z[v]$, so $(\underline H_x,\underline H_x)\in 1+v\mathbb Z[v]$.

**The standard pairing (6) and conclusion.** By (4) the form $(-,-)$ is the $A$-bilinear form whose matrix in the normalized standard basis $\{H_x\}$ is the identity; the published type-A Soergel Hom formula uses the standard pairing with $\langle H_x,H_y\rangle=\delta_{xy}$ on that normalized basis, and the dictionary of [F4] fixes the normalization $H_x=v^{\ell(x)}T_x$ and the resulting Kazhdan-Lusztig coefficients, so the transported pairing agrees with $(-,-)$ on the basis and hence on $H$ by bilinearity. All six clauses are proved over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$, using only existence and triangularity of the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis and no positivity and no choice.

citations.quote: Over $k=\mathbb Q$ or $k=\mathbb R$, the bimodule Soergel category has unique finite Krull-Schmidt decompositions. For every $x\in S_n$ there is a unique normalized indecomposable $B_x$ supported on $\{y:y\le x\}$ with top $\Delta$ layer exactly $\Delta_x=R_x(-\ell(x))$. It is the unique summand with the $x$ graph of any reduced Bott-Samelson word for $x$. Every indecomposable is exactly one $B_x(d)$. Its finite-dimensional degree-zero endomorphism algebra is local, with residue field $k$ under restriction to its rank-one top layer. No Kazhdan-Lusztig character identity is assumed.

Over $k=\mathbb Q$ or $\mathbb R$, let $B_x$ be the normalized indecomposable bimodule classified by its top support. With right dual $DM=\operatorname{Hom}_{-R}^{\bullet}(M,R)$, one has $DB_x\cong B_x$. Its right reduction has degrees only in $[-\ell(x),\ell(x)]$, all congruent to $\ell(x)$ modulo two, and the two extremal dimensions are one. Hence its reduced graded dimensions are symmetric. Every Bott-Samelson word has a graded perfect symmetric invariant trace form. These assertions assume neither the Kazhdan-Lusztig character conjecture nor hard Lefschetz.

For a reflection $t=(a\,b)$ with $a<b$, fix the hyperplane equation $c_t:=\beta_{ab}=x_a-x_b$ of [[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]]. For $y\in S_n$ put $p_y:=\prod_{t:\,yt<y}c_t\in R$. Let $M$ be a
Bott–Samelson bimodule or a direct summand of one, with its support submodules
$\Gamma_yM\subseteq\Gamma_{\le y}M\subseteq M$ and
$\Gamma_yM\subseteq\Gamma_{\ge y}M\subseteq M$ and the $y$-layer quotients
$\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M=\Gamma_{\le y}M/\Gamma_{<y}M$ and
$\underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M=\Gamma_{\ge y}M/\Gamma_{>y}M$ of
[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]], and
write $\Gamma^yM:=M/\Gamma_{\ne y}M$ for Soergel's $y$-layer quotient. Then:

1. the natural morphism $\Gamma_yM\to\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M$, the
   inclusion of the $y$-layer into the lower support submodule followed by the
   quotient map, is injective with image the submodule
   $p_y\cdot\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M$ obtained as the image of right
   multiplication by $p_y$, so it becomes an isomorphism after inverting $p_y$,
   that is $\Gamma_yM\cong(\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M)p_y$, and the $y$-layer
   is generated by the lower $y$-layer after inverting the hyperplane equations
   of the reflections $t$ with $yt<y$;
2. dually, the natural morphism $\underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M\to\Gamma^yM=M/\Gamma_{\ne y}M$
   is injective with image the image $p_y\cdot\Gamma^yM$ of right multiplication
   by $p_y$, so it becomes an isomorphism after the same inversion, that is
   $\underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M\cong(\Gamma^yM)p_y$ and the upper $y$-layer is
   determined by the $y$-layer quotient after inverting $p_y$;
3. in particular the graded ranks satisfy
   $\operatorname{rk}\Gamma_yM=\sum_\nu(M:\nabla_y(\nu))v^{\ell(y)-\nu}$ and
   $\operatorname{rk}\Gamma^yM=\sum_\nu(M:\Delta_y(\nu))v^{-\ell(y)-\nu}$, so
   that each graded rank determines the corresponding $y$-multiplicities of its support flag.

The inclusion chains displayed above are two separate chains: the lower and the
upper support submodule are not nested in general, and because the cutoffs of
[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]] are the
Bruhat principal sets $\{x:x\le y\}$ and $\{x:x\ge y\}$ of Soergel's
Notation 6.1, their intersection is exactly
$\Gamma_yM=\Gamma_{\le y}M\cap\Gamma_{\ge y}M$. This is Soergel's Satz 6.6 in
the notation of his Notation 6.1; the localization input is his Lemma 6.10, quoted in the Facts
block, and the rank identities are the computation of Satz 6.6's proof.

Let $M$ be a graded $R$-bimodule lying in $F_\Delta\cap F_\nabla$, so that it
carries a $\Delta$-flag and a $\nabla$-flag. Then:

1. the graded multiplicities $(M:\Delta_x(d))$ and $(M:\nabla_x(d))$ of
   [[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]] are
   independent of the compatible enumeration of the flag, so that the character
   sums $h_\Delta(M)$ and $h_\nabla(M)$ are functions of $M$ alone;
2. if $M=M'\oplus M''$ with $M',M''\in F_\Delta\cap F_\nabla$, then
   $(M:\Delta_x(d))=(M':\Delta_x(d))+(M'':\Delta_x(d))$ and likewise for
   $\nabla$; more generally the same holds for any direct summand $N$ of $M$
   which itself lies in $F_\Delta\cap F_\nabla$.

Let $M,N$ be objects of the type-A Soergel category $\mathrm{SBim}_n$, that is,
graded direct summands of finite direct sums of shifts of Bott–Samelson
bimodules $B_{i_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RB_{i_r}$ (the idempotent completion
of the Bott–Samelson category of [[def-the-type-a-soergel-category]]). Then
$\operatorname{Hom}_{R\text{-}R}(M,N)$ is a graded free $R$-module of graded
rank
$$\operatorname{rk}\operatorname{Hom}_{R\text{-}R}(M,N)=\sum_{x,d,e} (M:\Delta_x(d))\,(N:\nabla_x(e))\,v^{d-e},$$
which under the Hecke normalization $T_x\mapsto$ the standard basis of
[[def-type-a-hecke-algebra-in-soergel-normalization]] is the standard pairing
$\langle h_\Delta(M),h_\nabla(N)\rangle$ of the two characters with
$\langle\widetilde T_x,\widetilde T_y\rangle=\delta_{xy}$. In particular
$\operatorname{Hom}(M,M)$ is free of the same rank, and
$\operatorname{End}_{R\text{-}R}(R)=R$ is generated in degree $0$.

Let $M$ be a graded $R$-bimodule in $F_\Delta\cap F_\nabla$, so that by
[[lem-type-a-support-filtration-multiplicities-are-intrinsic]] the
multiplicities $(M:\Delta_x(d))$, $(M:\nabla_x(d))$ and the characters
$h_\Delta(M),h_\nabla(M)$ are defined and intrinsic. Then for every simple
reflection $s=s_i$:

1. $B_i\otimes_RM$ and $M\otimes_RB_i$ lie in $F_\Delta\cap F_\nabla$, with
   finitely many flag quotients;
2. $h_\Delta(B_i\otimes_RM)=H_i\,h_\Delta(M)$ and
   $h_\nabla(B_i\otimes_RM)=H_i\,h_\nabla(M)$, where
   $H_i=v(T_i+1)=\widetilde T_i+v$ and $\widetilde T_x=v^{\ell(x)}T_x$ is the
   normalized basis of [[lem-type-a-hecke-standard-basis-for-soergel-comparison]];
3. for the internal shift and all $k\in\mathbb Z$,
   $h_\Delta(M\{k\})=v^{-k}h_\Delta(M)$ and
   $h_\nabla(M\{k\})=v^{k}h_\nabla(M)$; in the Elias–Williamson notation of the
   sources, whose shift $(1)=\{-1\}$ lowers every generating degree by one,
   this says that $(1)$ multiplies $h_\Delta$ by $v$ and $h_\nabla$ by
   $v^{-1}$;
4. on $M=R$ the recursion reads $h_\Delta(B_i)=h_\nabla(B_i)=H_i$.

This is a statement about the action of the generators only: multiplicativity of
$h_\Delta$ and $h_\nabla$ for arbitrary tensor products is proved on this page
only after the categorification theorem.

Let $\underline i=(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ be a word in simple reflections and
$B_{\underline i}:=B_{i_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RB_{i_r}$, with
$B_\emptyset=R$. Then $B_{\underline i}$ belongs to both $F_\Delta$ and
$F_\nabla$: it has a $\Delta$-flag and a $\nabla$-flag in the sense of
[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]], its
support is contained in $Gr(S_n)$, and each successive quotient of these flags
is a standard bimodule $R_x\{a\}$ with $x$ a product
$x=s_{i_{j_1}}\cdots s_{i_{j_m}}$ ($1\le j_1<\cdots<j_m\le r$) of a
subexpression of $\underline i$ formed by keeping $m$ letters; the Coxeter
length $\ell(x)$ can be smaller than $m$. The shift $a$ of an occurrence
is computed recursively, one step $\pm1$ per letter of $\underline i$, from the
two rank-one exact sequences of step 1.2 below: the $\Delta$-chart and the
$\nabla$-chart use the two different sequences, so the shift depends on the
chosen subexpression and on the chart, and it is *not* a function of the lengths
and descent numbers of the subexpression alone: for the one-letter word $(s)$
the $\nabla$-chart occurrences are $R\{1\}$ and $R_s\{-1\}$, while the
$\Delta$-chart occurrences are the translates $\Delta_e(1)=R\{-1\}$ and
$\Delta_s(0)=R_s\{1\}$ of the same two subexpressions, so the same subexpression
carries different shifts in the two charts. In particular the number of occurrences of a graph $x$ in the
$\Delta$-flag and in the $\nabla$-flag of $B_{\underline i}$ is the number of
subexpressions of $\underline i$ with product $x$. Moreover $B_{\underline i}$
is finite free of rank $2^r$ as a left
$R$-module and as a right $R$-module, and the flag categories are closed under
tensoring with a generator on either side: if $M\in F_\Delta$ then
$B_s\otimes_RM\in F_\Delta$ and $M\otimes_RB_s\in F_\Delta$, and likewise with
$\nabla$ in place of $\Delta$.

For each $w\in S_n$ there is a unique element $\underline H_w\in H_v(n)$ with (i) $\overline{\underline H_w}=\underline H_w$ and (ii) $\underline H_w\in H_w+\sum_{y<w}v\mathbb Z[v]\,H_y$ (the sum over the lower Bruhat ideal of $w$). The elements $\{\underline H_w\}_{w\in S_n}$ form an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$, and writing $\underline H_w=\sum_{y\le w}p_{y,w}H_y$ one has $p_{w,w}=1$, $p_{y,w}=0$ unless $y\le w$, $p_{y,w}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ for $y<w$, the bar-duality $p_{x,w}=\sum_{y}r_{x,y}\,\overline{p_{y,w}}$ (matrix form $P=R\bar P$), and the symmetry $p_{y^{-1},w^{-1}}=p_{y,w}$. Moreover for $y<w$, with $d=\ell(w)-\ell(y)$: $p_{y,w}=v^{d}+\text{terms of strictly smaller degree}$ and $p_{y,w}\in v^{d}\,\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$; every $p_{y,w}$ has integer coefficients and fixed parity $d\bmod 2$.

Let $s=s_i$ be a simple reflection and $w\in S_n$. In the Kazhdan–Lusztig basis $\{\underline H_w\}$ of [[lem-type-a-kazhdan-lusztig-basis-has-elementary-triangular-bar-properties]]: $$\underline H_s\,\underline H_w=\begin{cases}(v+v^{-1})\,\underline H_w,&sw<w,\\[2pt] \underline H_{sw}+\displaystyle\sum_{\substack{z\in S_n\\ sz<z<w}}\mu(z,w)\,\underline H_z,&sw>w,\end{cases}$$ and symmetrically $\underline H_w\underline H_s=(v+v^{-1})\underline H_w$ if $ws<w$, $\underline H_w\underline H_s=\underline H_{ws}+\sum_{zs<z<w}\mu(z,w)\underline H_z$ if $ws>w$. Here $\mu(z,w)$ is the coefficient of $v$ in $p_{z,w}$ ([[def-kazhdan-lusztig-polynomials-in-the-classical-q-normalization]]), which can be nonzero only when $\ell(w)-\ell(z)$ is odd; the sums are finite since $S_n$ is finite. In particular $\underline H_s\underline H_s=(v+v^{-1})\underline H_s$, and $\underline H_s\underline H_w=\underline H_{sw}$ when $sw>w$ and $\ell(w)\le1$. The span conclusion is for the ascent case $sw>w$: there, $\underline H_s\underline H_w$ lies in the span of $\underline H_{sw}$ and of the $\underline H_z$ with $z<w$ and $sz<z$.

derivations.claim: For finite right-free rational $M,N$, a homogeneous bimodule map is determined by the images of a finite right basis. In a fixed degree the finitely many left-generator commutation relations are finite linear equations with rational coefficients. Their kernel commutes with the flat field extension to $\mathbb R$. Thus every homogeneous Hom space, and its composition, commutes with extension. The support cut on a specified graph union is the common kernel of its finitely generated graph ideal acting on the carrier: the carrier is right-free and generically a sum of reduced graph modules, so the relations hold before localization by torsion-freeness. These kernels commute with flat extension as well. Therefore the canonical support submodules, quotients, graph generator degrees and multiplicities commute with extension. Right reduction commutes with it by tensor associativity and the augmentation map.

Let $A=\operatorname{End}^0(B_x)$ over $\mathbb Q$. By [F1] it is finite-dimensional local with residue $\mathbb Q$, and its maximal ideal $J$ is nilpotent by the finite-algebra proof there. Step 1.1 gives $\operatorname{End}^0(B_x^R)=A\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb R$. The ideal $J\otimes\mathbb R$ is nilpotent and its quotient is $\mathbb R$; an element with nonzero residue is invertible by a finite geometric series after subtracting its scalar part. Hence this algebra is local with residue $\mathbb R$, and $B_x^R$ is indecomposable. Its top support layer is unchanged by step 1.1, so the real classification [F1] identifies it with the same normalized real label. Every real word is the extension of its rational word and its rational finite decomposition; the real classification and uniqueness imply that all real indecomposables and all real decompositions are the corresponding labels and shifts.

Duality exchanges the $\Delta$ and $
abla$ flags: dualize their right-split canonical layer sequences, which reverses order and the homogeneous degrees of their graph generators. A $\Delta_y(d)$ layer dualizes to $
abla_y(-d)$. Therefore normalized self-duality gives $h_\Delta(B_y)=h_
abla(B_y)$ by the weight conventions. The same is true for $B_xB_s$: an invariant isomorphism $B_x	o DB_x$ can be extended by the induced rank-one form construction in [F2], whose mixed-basis matrix has determinant one and yields an invariant isomorphism $B_xB_s	o D(B_xB_s)$. If $S(y)$ holds, both characters of $B_y$ are consequently $\underline H_y$. By [F3],[F4], its endomorphism Hom rank has no negative powers and constant term one. Since the polynomial ring has degree-zero part $\mathbb R$ and no negative degrees, its degree-zero endomorphism algebra is then exactly $\mathbb R$.

Step 1.1 proves the support multiplicity, character, Hom and reduction identities in (3). These characters have integer Laurent coefficients recording finite homogeneous graph bases; equality over the real category therefore gives the same integer coefficient equality over the rational category. No injectivity assertion about an unrelated extension of the coefficient ring is needed.

For $xs>x$, assume $S(y)$ for every $y<xs$, including $x$. The tensor $M=B_xB_s$ is a summand of the reduced word for $xs$. Its top layer is the word's unique $\Delta_{xs}$, because the reduced word for $x$ decomposes as $B_x$ and lower-support summands, whose tensor with $B_s$ cannot reach length $\ell(xs)$. By [F1] its unique top summand is therefore $B_{xs}$ unshifted and once; the other summands are $B_y(d)$ with $y<xs$. This top-layer argument makes no substitution of the unknown character of $B_{xs}$.

The character of $M$ is $\underline H_x\underline H_s$, and its standard expansion lies in $\mathbb Z[v]$: the only $v^{-1}$ in simple multiplication multiplies a strictly lower coefficient already divisible by $v$, while the top coefficient is on an ascent. For every lower $y$, the two Hom ranks $\operatorname{Hom}(B_y,M)$ and $\operatorname{Hom}(M,B_y)$ are the standard pairings of this polynomial character with $\underline H_y$, using self-duality from step 3.1. Hence they have no negative powers, and both Hom spaces have no negative-degree maps. A summand $B_y(d)$ with $d>0$ gives a negative-degree inclusion from unshifted $B_y$, and one with $d<0$ gives a negative-degree projection to it, by the convention $M(d)_i=M_{i+d}$. Both are impossible. Thus every lower summand is unshifted, proving the ascent statement with its actual nonnegative multiplicities $a_y$. The character of the top summand is not yet required to equal $\underline H_{xs}$, and no equality $a_y=\mu(y,x)$ is inferred.

For $xs<x$ and $S(x)$, the support of $M=B_xB_s$ stays at most $x$: take a reduced word for $x$ ending in $s$; toggling its last letter shows that the graphs $y,ys$ for $y\le x$ stay in this Bruhat interval. Its character is $(v+v^{-1})\underline H_x$ by [F4],[F5], so its top $x$ layer has the two shifts $\Delta_x(1),\Delta_x(-1)$. The maximal-layer splitting proof of [F1] splits off exactly $B_x(1)$ and $B_x(-1)$. Under $S(x)$ their characters already sum to the whole character of $M$. Any remaining nonzero summand would have a nonzero graph layer with a positive integral multiplicity, contradicting its zero character. Thus $M=B_x(1)\oplus B_x(-1)$ with no other summands, without assuming $S$ for any other label.

The local algebra and real indecomposability are step 2.1, and the degree-zero scalar assertion under $S(x)$ is step 3.1. Step 2.1 proves classification after extension, step 3.2 proves all base-change identities, and steps 3.3–4.2 prove the two decompositions with their exact stated hypotheses. Normalization and self-duality come from [F2], proved before the character comparisons.

citations.quote: Let $B_w$ be the rational indecomposable type-A Soergel bimodule and let $B_w^R$ be its real scalar extension. (1) $B_w^R$ is indecomposable; its finite-dimensional degree-zero endomorphism algebra is local with residue field $\mathbb R$. If $S(w)$ holds, its degree-zero endomorphism algebra is $\mathbb R$, but no rank-one assertion for the full graded endomorphism module is made. (2) Real extension preserves the labels and shifts of all finite Krull-Schmidt decompositions of rational Soergel bimodules, and every real indecomposable is a unique $B_w^R(d)$. (3) $\Delta$/$\nabla$ support-filtration multiplicities, characters, reduction by positive-degree right polynomials, and Hom spaces commute with scalar extension; thus character identities over $\mathbb R$ descend to $\mathbb Q$. (4) If $xs>x$ and $S(y)$ holds for all $y<xs$, then $B_xB_s=B_{xs}\oplus\bigoplus_{y<xs}B_y^{a_y}$ with $a_y$ nonnegative integers and no grading shifts; the top summand occurs once. If $xs<x$ and $S(x)$ holds, then $B_xB_s=B_x(1)\oplus B_x(-1)$. All assertions concern the normalized self-dual indecomposables.

For each simple reflection $s_i$ the graded $(R,R)$-bimodule $B_i$ is free of
rank two as a left $R$-module and free of rank two as a right $R$-module, with
left basis $\{1\otimes1,\,1\otimes\alpha_i\}$ and right basis
$\{1\otimes1,\,\alpha_i\otimes1\}$, both of degrees $-1$ and $1$; and every
Bott–Samelson tensor product $B_{i_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RB_{i_r}$ is finite
free as a left $R$-module and finite free as a right $R$-module.

**The operator.** Fix $x\in S_n$, a simple reflection $s$, a strictly dominant
$\rho\in S_2$ ([[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]])
and a real parameter $\zeta\ge0$. On the tensor product
$B_x^RB_s^R=B_x^R\otimes_SB_s^R$ define
$$L_\zeta:=(\rho\cdot(-))\otimes\mathrm{id}_{B_s^R}+\mathrm{id}_{B_x^R}\otimes(\zeta\,\rho\cdot(-)),$$
where the first summand is left multiplication by $\rho$ on the first factor and
the second summand is left multiplication by $\zeta\rho$ on the second factor.
Because the polynomial ring is commutative and the balanced tensor product
identifies $b r\otimes c=b\otimes rc$ for $r\in S$, the second summand equals
right multiplication by $\zeta\rho$ on the first factor; both summands are
degree-two, $S$-linear on the right, and commute, so $L_\zeta$ is a degree-two
right-$S$-linear endomorphism of $B_x^RB_s^R$. In particular $L_\zeta$ preserves
the submodule $MS_+$ for $M=B_x^RB_s^R$ and therefore descends to a degree-two
$\mathbb R$-linear endomorphism of the reduced module
$\overline{B_x^RB_s^R}$ ([[def-invariant-intersection-form-on-a-bott-samelson-bimodule]]
supplies the induced invariant form and the reduction conventions of
[[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]] apply).

**Symmetry.** Each summand of $L_\zeta$ is multiplication by an element in the
commutative position algebra of the tensor product: the first is multiplication
by $\rho$ on the first factor, the second is right (equivalently middle)
multiplication by $\zeta\rho$, which is self-adjoint for the induced invariant
form by the invariance identities of the form. Hence $L_\zeta$ is symmetric for
the induced form, and the Lefschetz forms $(\ ,\ )^{-i}_{L_\zeta}$ and the
primitive subspaces $P^{-i}_{L_\zeta}$ are those of
[[def-primitive-subspaces-hard-lefschetz-and-hodge-riemann-signs]] for this
operator.

**The deformation statements.** Write $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)_\zeta$,
$\mathrm{HR}(x,s)_\zeta$ and $\mathrm{HRbar}(x,s)_\zeta$ for centered hard
Lefschetz, the Hodge-Riemann relations and the strong embedded-form statement on
$\overline{B_x^RB_s^R}$ for the operator $L_\zeta$, with the bottom degree
$-\ell(x)-1$ and the standard sign
$(-1)^{(\ell(x)+1-i)/2}$ of the dictionary in
[[def-primitive-subspaces-hard-lefschetz-and-hodge-riemann-signs]]; the
definitions of $\mathrm{HR}(x,s)_\zeta$ and $\mathrm{HRbar}(x,s)_\zeta$ refer to
a fixed reduced-word induced form respectively to all choices of such forms.
At $\zeta=0$ the operator $L_0=\rho\cdot(-)\otimes\mathrm{id}$ is left
multiplication by $\rho$ on the first factor, so the zero-parameter statements
$\mathrm{hL}(x,s)_0$, $\mathrm{HR}(x,s)_0$, $\mathrm{HRbar}(x,s)_0$ are exactly
the undeformed statements $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)$, $\mathrm{HR}(x,s)$,
$\mathrm{HRbar}(x,s)$ of the dictionary. For fixed data the family
$\zeta\mapsto L_\zeta$ is polynomial of degree one in $\zeta$.

**Summand stability.** Any direct summand $B\subseteq B_x^RB_s^R$ that is a
sub-bimodule is stable under $L_0$, because left multiplication by the central
element $\rho$ is a bimodule endomorphism; stability under $L_\zeta$ for
$\zeta>0$ is a separate condition, since a projector onto $B$ need not commute
with the middle-position operator. The undeformed summand implications used in
the induction of this page are supplied by the local restriction lemma later on
this page, after deforming the parameter back to $\zeta=0$; no statement of this
definition identifies a restricted positive-parameter operator with a
restriction of $L_\zeta$.

Let $s=s_i$ be a simple reflection and $w\in S_n$. In the Kazhdan–Lusztig basis $\{\underline H_w\}$ of [[lem-type-a-kazhdan-lusztig-basis-has-elementary-triangular-bar-properties]]: $$\underline H_s\,\underline H_w=\begin{cases}(v+v^{-1})\,\underline H_w,&sw<w,\\[2pt] \underline H_{sw}+\displaystyle\sum_{\substack{z\in S_n\\ sz<z<w}}\mu(z,w)\,\underline H_z,&sw>w,\end{cases}$$ and symmetrically $\underline H_w\underline H_s=(v+v^{-1})\underline H_w$ if $ws<w$, $\underline H_w\underline H_s=\underline H_{ws}+\sum_{zs<z<w}\mu(z,w)\underline H_z$ if $ws>w$. Here $\mu(z,w)$ is the coefficient of $v$ in $p_{z,w}$ ([[def-kazhdan-lusztig-polynomials-in-the-classical-q-normalization]]), which can be nonzero only when $\ell(w)-\ell(z)$ is odd; the sums are finite since $S_n$ is finite. In particular $\underline H_s\underline H_s=(v+v^{-1})\underline H_s$, and $\underline H_s\underline H_w=\underline H_{sw}$ when $sw>w$ and $\ell(w)\le1$. The span conclusion is for the ascent case $sw>w$: there, $\underline H_s\underline H_w$ lies in the span of $\underline H_{sw}$ and of the $\underline H_z$ with $z<w$ and $sz<z$.

derivations.claim: **A genuine bimodule section.** Put $U=M\otimes_{S^s}S$, so $MB_s=U(1)$. The actual bimodule decomposition of [F1] gives $U\cong M\oplus M(-2)$. The multiplication counit $c:U\to M$, $c(b\otimes r)=br$, is an $S$-bimodule map. The bottom degree of $U$ is the single line $M^{-\ell(x)}\otimes1$, on which $c$ is nonzero. Only the unshifted summand $M$ in this decomposition has that degree, so $c$ restricts to a nonzero degree-zero endomorphism of that summand. By [F1] it is a nonzero scalar, hence invertible. Compose its inverse with the actual bimodule inclusion to obtain a degree-zero bimodule section $\sigma:M\to U$. On the bottom line $\sigma(b)=b\otimes1$, because $c\sigma=1$ and that line in $U$ is one dimensional.

**The twisted counit.** Define $c_s:U\to M_s$ by $c_s(b\otimes r)=b\,s(r)$. It is balanced over $S^s$, left $S$-linear and right-$s$-semilinear. Since the section $\sigma$ in step 1.1 is genuinely right-$S$-linear, $t=c_s\sigma:M\to M$ is degree zero, left $S$-linear and right-$s$-semilinear. It is the identity on the bottom line by step 1.1. This argument uses the actual bimodule summand, rather than the generally non-right-linear map $b\mapsto b\otimes1$.

**The involution property of $t$.** Since $t$ is right-$s$-semilinear and degree zero, $t^2$ is an ordinary degree-zero $S$-bimodule endomorphism of $M$, hence a scalar by $\operatorname{End}^0(M)=\mathbb R$; its scalar is $1$ because $t^2$ acts as the identity on the one-dimensional bottom degree by step 2.1. Hence $t^2=\mathrm{id}_M$.

**The descent isomorphism.** For $u\in U$ one has $c_s(u)-c(u)\in M\alpha_s$, because $s(r)-r\in\alpha_s S$ for every $r\in S$; consequently $t(m)-m\in M\alpha_s$ for every $m\in M$. Define $N:=\{m\in M: t(m)=m\}$. Every $m$ splits as $m=\tfrac12(m+t(m))+\tfrac12(m-t(m))$ into an invariant and an anti-invariant part, and an anti-invariant $m$ (that is, $t(m)=-m$) lies in $M\alpha_s$, say $m=n\alpha_s$; since right multiplication by $\alpha_s$ is injective by [F2] and $t(m)=-m$ with $s(\alpha_s)=-\alpha_s$ gives $t(n\alpha_s)=t(n)s(\alpha_s)=-t(n)\alpha_s$ and hence $t(n)=n$, we get $n\in N$ and the anti-invariant part of $m$ is $N\alpha_s$. Therefore $M=N\oplus N\alpha_s$ as $(S,S^s)$-bimodules, and the multiplication map induces an isomorphism $N\otimes_{S^s}S\to M$; this proves the descent isomorphism.

**The matrix of $L_\zeta$.** Use the proved descent $M=N\otimes_{S^s}S$ to write $MB_s=N\otimes_{S^s}S\otimes_{S^s}S(1)$. Splitting the middle factor by $S=S^s\oplus(\alpha_s/2)S^s$ gives the bimodule isomorphism $MB_s\cong M(1)\oplus M(-1)$, with structure maps $\iota_1,\iota_2,\pi_1,\pi_2$ of [F2] satisfying $\pi_a\iota_b=\delta_{ab}$. In this basis, middle multiplication by $\rho$ has entries $\pi_1(\rho)$, $\pi_1(\alpha_s\rho)/2$, $\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)$ and $\partial_s(\alpha_s\rho)/2$, and the operators of multiplication by $\rho$ on the two outer factors contribute the same diagonal $\rho\cdot(-)$ on $M(1)$ and $M(-1)$. All entries except the off-diagonal $\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)$ have positive polynomial degree in $\rho$ and vanish after the right reduction; the off-diagonal entry has the constant term $\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)$ and contributes the degree-two map $\zeta\rho(\alpha_s^\vee):M(1)\to M(-1)$; hence, after reduction, $L_\zeta$ is the displayed matrix.

**Hard Lefschetz for $\zeta>0$.** Assume $\mathrm{hL}(x)$, so the reduced module $\overline M$ is a direct sum of centered $\rho$-strings $u_0,\ldots,u_m$ with $\deg u_j=-m+2j$ and $\rho u_j=u_{j+1}$; on each string, left multiplication by $\rho$ is the standard nilpotent Jordan block. In the two-dimensional middle factor with basis $v_-,v_+$ of degrees $-1,+1$ and $e(v_-)=\zeta\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)v_+$, $e(v_+)=0$, the operator $e=L_\zeta$ on the string tensor $\bigoplus_j u_j\otimes\{v_-,v_+\}$ acts by $e^k(u_jv_-)=u_{j+k}v_-+k\,u_{j+k-1}v_+$ and $e^k(u_jv_+)=u_{j+k}v_+$ (indices out of range zero), after normalizing the nonzero scalar $\zeta\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)$ to $1$ by rescaling $v_+$; for $0\le k\le m-1$ of the compatible parity $k\equiv m+1\pmod2$, in centered degree $-k$ the source basis $u_{(m+1-k)/2}v_-,\,u_{(m-1-k)/2}v_+$ and the corresponding target basis exhibit $e^k$ as a matrix with diagonal entries $1$ and $1$, lower-left entry $k$, and upper-right entry $0$, which is invertible; at $k=m+1$ the map sends $u_0v_-$ to $(m+1)u_mv_+$, nonzero by the normalization $\zeta\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)>0$. The operator on each string is thus an isomorphism in every centered degree, and $L_\zeta$ on the direct sum of strings satisfies hL. Positivity of $\zeta\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)$ uses $\zeta>0$ and strict dominance of $\rho$.

**Failure at $\zeta=0$ and conclusion.** At $\zeta=0$ the matrix of step 5.1 is diagonal with respect to the decomposition $MB_s=M(1)\oplus M(-1)$. The bottom class $b\in\overline M^{-\ell(x)}$ sits in the first summand in degree $-\ell(x)-1$ and satisfies $\rho^{\ell(x)+1}b=0$ because $\overline M^{\ell(x)+2}=0$; the opposite class in $M(-1)$ of degree $\ell(x)+1$ is nonzero by self-duality and dimension symmetry. Hence $\rho^{\ell(x)+1}$ is not injective on $\overline{MB_s}$ in the centered grading and centered hL fails at $\zeta=0$, even though the two individual shifted copies of $\overline M$ have their own strings centered at $\pm1$. Steps 1.1-5.1 prove the descent isomorphism and the matrix, step 6.1 the positive-parameter hard Lefschetz, and this step the failure at zero; no singular-category classification or character conjecture beyond $\mathrm{S}(x)$ is used.

boundaries.reason: The statement fixes the bimodule M and its two-term product MB_s = M(1) + M(-1); every index occurring in it is determined by that fixed pair, so there is no empty family to interpret.

boundaries.evidence: The zero parameter is one of the two regimes analysed: step 5.1 computes the matrix for general parameter, step 6.1 proves hard Lefschetz for positive parameter by rescaling, and step 7.1 exhibits the diagonal zero-parameter matrix whose bottom class fails injectivity.

The two multiplicity-one summands M(1) and M(-1) are isolated in steps 5.1 and 6.1, and the one-dimensional space spanned by the bottom class is what step 7.1 uses to detect the zero-parameter failure.

Degeneracy occurs exactly at the vanishing parameter: in step 7.1 the strict inequality defining the relevant Lefschetz map collapses when the scaling factor vanishes, and that collapse is what separates the two parameter regimes.

The internal-degree endpoints of the two summands drive the matrix computations: step 5.1 tracks the matrices of L_zeta on M(1) and M(-1), and step 7.1 evaluates the centred map at the bottom degree of the first summand.
Choice-free: the splitting of the invariant ring in step 1.1 is an explicit direct sum, the section sigma is defined by a formula in step 2.1, and the scalar t is computed in step 3.1.

$F_i\otimes_RF_i^{-1}\simeq R\simeq F_i^{-1}\otimes_RF_i$ in
$K^b(R^e\text{-grmod})$, where $R$ denotes the unit complex concentrated in
cohomological degree $0$ with zero differential. Explicitly, the signed tensor
totalization of $F_i$ and $F_i^{-1}$ has terms
$$B_i(-1)\ \longrightarrow\ B_i\otimes_RB_i\oplus R\ \longrightarrow\ B_i(1)$$
in cohomological degrees $-1,0,1$; the rank-one splitting
$B_i\otimes_RB_i\cong B_i(1)\oplus B_i(-1)$ exhibits two successive
invertible differential blocks. Gaussian elimination splits off two
contractible two-term complexes, leaving $R$ in degree $0$.
The same argument with the factors exchanged gives
$F_i^{-1}\otimes_RF_i\simeq R$. All scalars occurring in the contractions are
units $\varepsilon_i^{\pm1},2^{\pm1}\in\mathbb Q$, so the homotopy classes do
not depend on the signs of the chosen normalization.

Let $t,u$ be signed words for the same braid $v$. Then the normalized map
$$\gamma_{t,u}\colon F(t)\longrightarrow F(u)$$
of [[lem-rouquier-derived-comparisons-give-unique-normalized-homotopy-maps]]
is a canonical homotopy equivalence, natural with respect to the multiplication
maps: for every other braid $v'$ with chosen words $t',u'$, the diagrams
comparing $F(t)\otimes_RF(t')$ with $F(u)\otimes_RF(u')$ commute up to the
canonical associativity isomorphisms, and $\gamma_{t,u}$ is the unique homotopy
class with the prescribed derived image $c_{t,u}$. Consequently the object
$G_v$ of [[thm-rouquier-complexes-form-a-coherent-braid-group-action]] is
independent of the chosen representative up to canonical homotopy equivalence,
and the notation $F(\beta)$ for the Rouquier complex of a braid element is well
defined up to canonical isomorphism in $K^b(R^e\text{-grmod})$; this is an
isomorphism statement in the homotopy category, not an equality of complexes.

Let $B_w$ be the rational indecomposable type-A Soergel bimodule and let $B_w^R$ be its real scalar extension. (1) $B_w^R$ is indecomposable; its finite-dimensional degree-zero endomorphism algebra is local with residue field $\mathbb R$. If $S(w)$ holds, its degree-zero endomorphism algebra is $\mathbb R$, but no rank-one assertion for the full graded endomorphism module is made. (2) Real extension preserves the labels and shifts of all finite Krull-Schmidt decompositions of rational Soergel bimodules, and every real indecomposable is a unique $B_w^R(d)$. (3) $\Delta$/$\nabla$ support-filtration multiplicities, characters, reduction by positive-degree right polynomials, and Hom spaces commute with scalar extension; thus character identities over $\mathbb R$ descend to $\mathbb Q$. (4) If $xs>x$ and $S(y)$ holds for all $y<xs$, then $B_xB_s=B_{xs}\oplus\bigoplus_{y<xs}B_y^{a_y}$ with $a_y$ nonnegative integers and no grading shifts; the top summand occurs once. If $xs<x$ and $S(x)$ holds, then $B_xB_s=B_x(1)\oplus B_x(-1)$. All assertions concern the normalized self-dual indecomposables.

**The construction.** For a signed word
$$\sigma=\sigma_{i_1}^{\epsilon_1}\cdots\sigma_{i_r}^{\epsilon_r},\qquad \epsilon_k\in\{\pm1\},\ 1\le i_k\le n-1,$$
put
$$F(\sigma):=F_{i_1}^{\epsilon_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RF_{i_r}^{\epsilon_r},$$
the iterated signed tensor totalization of
[[def-bounded-complex-of-graded-bimodules-and-signed-tensor-totalization]] of
the Rouquier generator complexes of
[[def-positive-and-negative-rouquier-generator-complexes]], bracketed left to
right; the empty word ($r=0$) is sent to the unit complex $R$ concentrated in
cohomological degree $0$. This is the **Rouquier complex of the word**. When
$\epsilon_k=+1$ the letter contributes the positive complex $F_{i_k}$ and when
$\epsilon_k=-1$ it contributes $F_{i_k}^{-1}$.

**Structure.** $F(\sigma)$ is a bounded cochain complex of graded
$(R,R)$-bimodules with degree-zero differentials, concentrated in cohomological
degrees $-r_-,\ldots,r_+$, where $r_-$ and $r_+$ count the negative and
positive letters: the term $F(\sigma)^m$ is the direct sum of the
$\binom{r}{m+r_-}$ tensor products of one term of each factor, since the
minimal choice has degree $-r_-$ and each upper-term choice adds one. It carries a
cohomological degree and an internal grading, and the differential is the
Koszul totalization differential. A positive letter contributes its unit term
$R(1)$ in cohomological degree $1$ and the internal shift $(1)$ to that term; a
negative letter contributes its unit term $R(-1)$ in cohomological degree $-1$
and the internal shift $(-1)$. Every term is a finite direct sum of finite tensor products of copies
of $R(\pm1)$ and $B_i$, hence is finite free on both sides
([[lem-type-a-soergel-generators-are-finite-free-on-both-sides]]), so each term
is finite graded projective as a left module and as a right module and $F(\sigma)$ defines a
derived tensor functor by
[[thm-a-bounded-projective-bimodule-complex-defines-a-derived-tensor-functor]].

**Status of the notation.** The notation records the chosen word $(\sigma)$
together with the chosen bracket; it asserts nothing about independence of the
word, of the sign normalization or of the bracketing. That the homotopy class
of $F(\sigma)$ depends only on the braid represented by $\sigma$ is the content
of [[thm-rouquier-complex-is-well-defined-up-to-canonical-homotopy-equivalence]],
whose proof uses the braid relations of the generator complexes and could not be
stated before those relations were proved.

**Convention for comparison.** The library's positive generator $F_i$ is
Rouquier's $F_{s_i}=[A\otimes_{A^{s_i}}A\to A]$ with the library external shift
$(1)$ on both terms, after giving the polynomial variables degree $2$:
$$F_i=[(R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R)(1)\longrightarrow R(1)].$$
Rouquier's negative complex of §3.2.4 becomes $F_i^{-1}$ after doubling
internal degrees and shifting the whole complex by $(-1)$, up to the unit
scalar coming from the root normalization. As recorded in
[[def-positive-and-negative-rouquier-generator-complexes]], the
complexes of Rouquier, Gorsky–Kivinen–Simental, Khovanov and Elias–Krasner
differ from $F_i$ and $F_i^{-1}$ by homological or internal shifts, so any
comparison with those sources is read through the dictionary recorded there.
The empty word corresponds to the trivial braid and to the identity functor.

Let $M$ be a graded $R$-bimodule in $F_\Delta\cap F_\nabla$, so that by
[[lem-type-a-support-filtration-multiplicities-are-intrinsic]] the
multiplicities $(M:\Delta_x(d))$, $(M:\nabla_x(d))$ and the characters
$h_\Delta(M),h_\nabla(M)$ are defined and intrinsic. Then for every simple
reflection $s=s_i$:

1. $B_i\otimes_RM$ and $M\otimes_RB_i$ lie in $F_\Delta\cap F_\nabla$, with
   finitely many flag quotients;
2. $h_\Delta(B_i\otimes_RM)=H_i\,h_\Delta(M)$ and
   $h_\nabla(B_i\otimes_RM)=H_i\,h_\nabla(M)$, where
   $H_i=v(T_i+1)=\widetilde T_i+v$ and $\widetilde T_x=v^{\ell(x)}T_x$ is the
   normalized basis of [[lem-type-a-hecke-standard-basis-for-soergel-comparison]];
3. for the internal shift and all $k\in\mathbb Z$,
   $h_\Delta(M\{k\})=v^{-k}h_\Delta(M)$ and
   $h_\nabla(M\{k\})=v^{k}h_\nabla(M)$; in the Elias–Williamson notation of the
   sources, whose shift $(1)=\{-1\}$ lowers every generating degree by one,
   this says that $(1)$ multiplies $h_\Delta$ by $v$ and $h_\nabla$ by
   $v^{-1}$;
4. on $M=R$ the recursion reads $h_\Delta(B_i)=h_\nabla(B_i)=H_i$.

This is a statement about the action of the generators only: multiplicativity of
$h_\Delta$ and $h_\nabla$ for arbitrary tensor products is proved on this page
only after the categorification theorem.

Over $k=\mathbb Q$ or $k=\mathbb R$, the bimodule Soergel category has unique finite Krull-Schmidt decompositions. Its finite-dimensional degree-zero endomorphism algebra is local, with residue field $k$ under restriction to its rank-one top layer. No Kazhdan-Lusztig character identity is assumed.

Let $n\ge1$ and $A:=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$. For $n\ge2$, define the **normalized type-A Hecke algebra** $H_v(n)$ to be the associative unital $A$-algebra presented by generators $H_{s_1},\ldots,H_{s_{n-1}}$ with relations
$$H_{s_i}^2=1+(v^{-1}-v)H_{s_i},\qquad H_{s_i}H_{s_{i+1}}H_{s_i}=H_{s_{i+1}}H_{s_i}H_{s_{i+1}},\qquad H_{s_i}H_{s_j}=H_{s_j}H_{s_i}\quad(|i-j|>1).$$
For $n=1$, set $H_v(1):=A$.

Here $S_n=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\ldots,n\})$, $s_i=(i\ i+1)$, and $\ell$ is inversion length as in [[def-symmetric-group]] and [[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]. For $w\in S_n$, let $T_w$ be the standard basis element of the generic Hecke algebra of [[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]], formed from any reduced expression of $w$, and after the coefficient specialization $q\mapsto v^{-2}$ put $H_w:=v^{\ell(w)}T_w$. Equivalently, $H_w=H_{s_{i_1}}\cdots H_{s_{i_k}}$ for a reduced expression $w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k}$. The standard-basis theorem [[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]] and rescaling by units show that $\{H_w:w\in S_n\}$ is an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$.

Right multiplication by a generator is
$$H_wH_{s_i}=H_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)+1,\qquad H_wH_{s_i}=H_{ws_i}+(v^{-1}-v)H_w\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)-1.$$

**Dictionary with the generic normalization.** If the generic parameter in [[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]] is denoted by $q$, its relation is $T_i^2=(q-1)T_i+q$. The coefficient map $q\mapsto v^{-2}$ is the stated specialization, and $H_{s_i}=vT_i$. This gives $H_{s_i}^2=1+(v^{-1}-v)H_{s_i}$; the braid and commutation relations are unchanged. The two multiplication cases above are the standard-basis rule after the same rescaling.

**Bar assignment.** Let $F$ be the free associative $\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$-algebra on the generator symbols. Define the semilinear algebra map $\iota_0:F\to F$ by $\iota_0(v)=v^{-1}$ and $\iota_0(H_{s_i})=H_{s_i}-(v^{-1}-v)$. In the quotient $H_v(n)$, the quadratic relation makes this latter element the two-sided inverse $H_{s_i}^{-1}$. The next lemma proves that $\iota_0$ preserves the defining ideal and descends to a well-defined involution $\iota$ on $H_v(n)$.

All items on this page use this normalization. It agrees with Elias–Williamson §3.2 under $H_x=v^{\ell(x)}T_x$ and $q=v^{-2}$.

For each $w\in S_n$ there is a unique element $\underline H_w\in H_v(n)$ with (i) $\overline{\underline H_w}=\underline H_w$ and (ii) $\underline H_w\in H_w+\sum_{y<w}v\mathbb Z[v]\,H_y$ (the sum over the lower Bruhat ideal of $w$). The elements $\{\underline H_w\}_{w\in S_n}$ form an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$, and writing $\underline H_w=\sum_{y\le w}p_{y,w}H_y$ one has $p_{w,w}=1$, $p_{y,w}=0$ unless $y\le w$, $p_{y,w}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ for $y<w$, the bar-duality $p_{x,w}=\sum_{y}r_{x,y}\,\overline{p_{y,w}}$ (matrix form $P=R\bar P$), and the symmetry $p_{y^{-1},w^{-1}}=p_{y,w}$. Moreover for $y<w$, with $d=\ell(w)-\ell(y)$: $p_{y,w}=v^{d}+\text{terms of strictly smaller degree}$ and $p_{y,w}\in v^{d}\,\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$; every $p_{y,w}$ has integer coefficients and fixed parity $d\bmod 2$.

Identify $\mathbb Z[q]$ with $\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$ by $q\mapsto v^{-2}$. For $y\le w$ in $S_n$, put $d=\ell(w)-\ell(y)$ and define the **Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomial** $P_{y,w}(q)\in\mathbb Z[q]$ by $$P_{y,w}(v^{-2})=v^{-d}p_{y,w},$$ where $\underline H_w=\sum_{y\le w}p_{y,w}H_y$ is the Kazhdan–Lusztig basis of [[lem-type-a-kazhdan-lusztig-basis-has-elementary-triangular-bar-properties]]. The parity clause of that theorem makes the right side a polynomial in $v^{-2}$. The conventions are: $P_{y,w}=0$ unless $y\le w$, $P_{w,w}=1$, $P_{y,w}$ has constant term 1, and for $y<w$ its degree is at most $(\ell(w)-\ell(y)-1)/2$. The **$\mu$-coefficient** is $$\mu(y,w):=	ext{coefficient of }q^{(\ell(w)-\ell(y)-1)/2}	ext{ in }P_{y,w},$$ defined to be 0 when $\ell(w)-\ell(y)$ is even; equivalently $\mu(y,w)$ is the coefficient of $v$ in $p_{y,w}$. One writes $\mu(y|w)
e0$ when $y
e w$ and ($y<w$ and $\mu(y,w)
e0$) or ($w<y$ and $\mu(w,y)
e0$). The dictionary with the literature is recorded for use: with the classical parameter $T_s^2=(q-1)T_s+q$ one has $H_w=v^{\ell(w)}T_w$, the element $\underline H_w$ is the basis element $C'_w$ of [EW], and $h_{y,w}=p_{y,w}$ with $v^{\ell(w)-\ell(y)}P_{y,w}(v^{-2})=h_{y,w}$ [EW, Remark 3.2].

**The category and its radical.** Let $\mathcal B=\mathrm{SBim}_n^R$ be the real
graded type-A Soergel category of
[[def-real-type-a-soergel-category-and-scalar-extension]], with degree-zero
morphisms; it is a graded additive idempotent-complete category
([[def-additive-category]], [[def-the-idempotent-completion-of-a-preadditive-category]])
whose objects are finite direct sums of shifts of the indecomposables $B_w^R$
([[lem-rational-and-real-type-a-soergel-characters-and-indecomposable-labels-agree]]).
Its **categorical radical** is the two-sided ideal
$$\operatorname{rad}\mathcal B:=\{f:M\to N\ :\ \text{for every }g:N\to M,\ 1_M-gf\text{ is invertible}\},$$
and $q:\mathcal B\to\mathcal B^{ss}:=\mathcal B/\operatorname{rad}\mathcal B$ is
the quotient functor. The radical is defined by the displayed invertibility
criterion and is not claimed to be nilpotent in general; on objects with local
endomorphism rings (as here, by the comparison lemma) it consists of the
non-units in the relevant endomorphism algebras.

**Minimal complexes.** Let $K^b(\mathcal B)$ be the homotopy category of bounded
cochain complexes of graded bimodules with degree-zero differentials
([[def-bounded-complex-of-graded-bimodules-and-signed-tensor-totalization]],
[[def-homotopy-category-of-chain-complexes]]). A bounded complex $F$ is
**minimal** when $q(d_F)=0$ in every degree, i.e. every differential of $F$
lies in the radical. Homological shifts are written $[j]$
([[def-shift-of-a-chain-complex]]); mapping cones are as in
[[def-mapping-cone-of-a-chain-map]]; contractibility and homotopies are as in
[[def-complex-homotopy-and-contractibility-in-an-additive-category]]; and the
two-term cancellation used on this page is
[[thm-homological-gaussian-elimination-splits-off-a-contractible-two-term-complex]]
with the block calculus of
[[def-invertible-differential-block-and-schur-complement-reduction]].

**Perverse bimodules.** Let $\underline H_x$ be the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis of the
Hecke algebra of the frontier Hecke page, transported to this page by the
comparison lemma. A Soergel bimodule is **perverse** when its character is a
nonnegative integer combination of the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis elements
$\underline H_x$ (not of the standard basis elements $H_x$); it is
**p-split** when its indecomposable summands are shifts of perverse ones. Thus
if $\mathrm{S}(x)$ holds then $B_x^R$ is perverse, since its character is
$\underline H_x$; no other perversity of a normalized indecomposable is asserted
before $\mathrm{S}(x)$.

**The perverse cuts.** Let $M$ be p-split and fix a decomposition
$$M=\bigoplus_{x,k}B_x^R(k)^{m_{x,k}}$$
with the normalized $B_x^R$ perverse (such a decomposition exists by the
comparison lemma, and the cuts below are proved intrinsic by the structural
lemma). For $j\in\mathbb Z$ set
$$\tau_{\le j}M:=\bigoplus_{k\ge -j}B_x^R(k)^{m_{x,k}},\qquad \tau_{<j}M:=\tau_{\le j-1}M,\qquad \tau_{\ge j}M:=M/\tau_{<j}M,$$
and define the associated graded
$$H^j(M):=\bigl(\tau_{\le j}M/\tau_{<j}M\bigr)(j),$$
so that the $j$-th perverse piece is normalized by the internal shift $(j)$.
Internal shifts $(d)$ change module degrees and homological shifts $[j]$ change
complex degrees; the two are kept distinct throughout.

**The perverse subcategories of complexes.** For a bounded complex
$F=(F^i,d^i)$ define
$$F\in pK^b_{\ge0}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F\ \text{is isomorphic in }K^b(\mathcal B)\ \text{to a complex with p-split terms and}\ \tau_{<-i}(F^i)=0\ \text{for all }i,$$
$$F\in pK^b_{\le0}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F\ \text{is isomorphic in }K^b(\mathcal B)\ \text{to a complex with p-split terms and}\ F^i=\tau_{\le-i}(F^i)\ \text{for all }i.$$
Equivalently, in the termwise decompositions the internal shifts $k$ satisfy
$k\le i$ for $pK^b_{\ge0}$ and $k\ge i$ for $pK^b_{\le0}$. The structural lemma
of this page supplies the semisimplicity of $\mathcal B^{ss}$, the existence and
uniqueness of minimal models, the intrinsicness and functoriality of the cuts,
their preservation under direct summands and their extension closure in
distinguished triangles; none of these properties is asserted by this
definition. The objects $pK^b_{\ge0}$ and $pK^b_{\le0}$ are the classes inside
which the Rouquier complexes of the next items are shown to lie, following the
orientation of Elias-Williamson Section 6.3.

(1) The quotient $\mathcal B^{ss}$ is semisimple with simple classes $B_x(k)$ and endomorphism rings $\mathbb R$, and $q$ reflects isomorphisms.

(2) Every bounded complex of $\mathcal B$ has a minimal direct summand whose inclusion is a homotopy equivalence, and any two minimal models are isomorphic as complexes.

(3) Every direct summand of a perverse (respectively p-split) bimodule is perverse (respectively p-split).

(4) For perverse $M,N$ one has $\operatorname{Hom}(M,N(-i))=0$ for $i>0$.

(5) The perverse cuts on p-split bimodules are independent of the chosen decomposition and are preserved by every morphism.

(6) The definitions of $pK^b_{\ge0}$ and $pK^b_{\le0}$ can equivalently be tested on the minimal model, and both classes are closed under extensions in distinguished triangles.

Let $\underline x$ be a reduced expression for $x\in S_n$ and let $F_{\underline x}$ be the Rouquier complex $F_{s_1}\cdots F_{s_m}$ (or its minimal subcomplex). Then for every $y\in S_n$ there is an isomorphism in the homotopy category of graded bimodules
$$\Gamma_{\ge y}(F_{\underline x})/\Gamma_{>y}(F_{\underline x})\;\cong\;\begin{cases}\Delta_x,&y=x,\\0,&y\ne x,\end{cases}$$
where $\Delta_x=R_x(-\ell(x))$. Equivalently: the Bruhat support subquotient of a positive Rouquier complex is contractible except in the top layer $\Delta_x$; $F_{\underline x}$ is $\Delta$-split in the sense that each of its support subquotients is a direct sum of standard bimodules, and the top layer is a single $\Delta_x$. No positivity of characters and no assumption $\mathrm{S}$ is used; the statement is unconditional for every finite type-$A$ Coxeter group and the coordinate reflection realization.

Let $M,N$ be objects of the type-A Soergel category $\mathrm{SBim}_n$, that is,
graded direct summands of finite direct sums of shifts of Bott–Samelson
bimodules $B_{i_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RB_{i_r}$ (the idempotent completion
of the Bott–Samelson category of [[def-the-type-a-soergel-category]]). Then
$\operatorname{Hom}_{R\text{-}R}(M,N)$ is a graded free $R$-module of graded
rank
$$\operatorname{rk}\operatorname{Hom}_{R\text{-}R}(M,N)=\sum_{x,d,e} (M:\Delta_x(d))\,(N:\nabla_x(e))\,v^{d-e},$$
which under the Hecke normalization $T_x\mapsto$ the standard basis of
[[def-type-a-hecke-algebra-in-soergel-normalization]] is the standard pairing
$\langle h_\Delta(M),h_\nabla(N)\rangle$ of the two characters with
$\langle\widetilde T_x,\widetilde T_y\rangle=\delta_{xy}$. In particular
$\operatorname{Hom}(M,M)$ is free of the same rank, and
$\operatorname{End}_{R\text{-}R}(R)=R$ is generated in degree $0$.

derivations.claim: **Base of the induction.** [base] For $x=e$ the Rouquier complex is the unit $S$ concentrated in cohomological degree $0$, so $^0F_e=S=B_e$, there is no term of index $i\ge1$, both perverse bounds hold trivially, and the only nonzero inverse coefficient is $g_{e,e}=1$; for $x=s_i$ the complex $F_{s_i}=[B_{s_i}^R\to S(1)]$ has $^0F_{s_i}=B_{s_i}$ and $^1F_{s_i}=S(1)=B_e^R(1)$ and no other term, so $m_{e,1}=1$ with $\ell(s_i)-\ell(e)=1\equiv1\pmod2$, $B_{s_i}$ is perverse by $\mathrm S(s_i)$ and $S(1)$ is the shift of the perverse unit, so $F_{s_i}\in pK^b_{\ge0}\cap pK^b_{\le0}$ and $g_{s_i,s_i}=1$, $g_{e,s_i}=-v$.

**Induction hypothesis and the last letter.** [ih] Fix $x\ne e$, write $\underline x=s_1\cdots s_m$ with $m\ge1$ and put $y=s_1\cdots s_{m-1}$, $s=s_m$, so that $x=ys$ with $\ell(x)=\ell(y)+1$; the hypothesis $\mathrm S(\le x)$ contains $\mathrm S(\le y)$, and we assume the three assertions of the statement for $y$: $^0F_y=B_y$, $^iF_y=\bigoplus_{z<y}B_z(i)^{m^y_{z,i}}$ for $i\ge1$, and $F_y\in pK^b_{\ge0}\cap pK^b_{\le0}$. By [F1], $F_x\cong F_yF_s$ in $K^b$.

**Descent contraction.** Let $z$ and a simple reflection $s$ satisfy $zs<z$ and $\mathrm S(z)$; then $B_zF_s\cong B_z(-1)$ in $K^b$. Indeed, by [F2] the two-term complex $B_zF_s$ has terms $B_zB_s=B_z(1)\oplus B_z(-1)$ in degree $0$ and $B_z(1)$ in degree $1$, with differential $d=(\delta,\eta)$ where $\delta\in\operatorname{End}^0(B_z(1))=\operatorname{End}^0(B_z)=\mathbb R$ by [F2] and [F6]. If $\delta=0$ then $B_zF_s$ is the direct sum of the two nonzero complexes $[B_z(1)\to0]$ and $[B_z(-1)\xrightarrow{\ \eta\ }B_z(1)]$, contradicting the indecomposability of $B_zF_s$, which is the image of the indecomposable $B_z$ under the equivalence $-\otimes F_s$; hence $\delta\ne0$ is an isomorphism, homological Gaussian elimination cancels the contractible two-term complex $B_z(1)\cong B_z(1)$, and the remainder is $B_z(-1)$ concentrated in degree $0$.

**Top support and the Euler character.** Every positive-degree term of the word complex omits at least one letter, so no such term has the $x$ graph by [F3]. The degree-zero term is its reduced word, whose top summand is exactly $B_x$ unshifted and once. Gaussian minimalization cannot remove it, since no target term has its label. Thus in the minimal complex $m^0_{x,0}=1$ and every other $m^i_{x,k}$ is zero, by actual support rather than alternating cancellation. Character additivity makes its Euler character unchanged by removing a contractible pair. The generator recursion and shift rule in [F3] give $\operatorname{ch}(F_zF_s)=\operatorname{ch}(F_z)(\underline H_s-v)$ degree by degree. Iterating along the reduced word therefore gives Euler character $H_x$. Under the stated $S(\le x)$, expanding each actual summand character in the KL basis yields $\sum_{i,k}(-1)^im^i_{w,k}v^k=g_{w,x}$. This equality is used only for the Euler coefficients, after the support proof of the top multiplicity.

**Ascent perverse bound.** Let $z\le y$ and a simple reflection $s$ satisfy $zs>z$; then $B_zF_s\in pK^b_{\ge0}$. Indeed, $\mathrm S(u)$ holds for every $u<zs$, because $u<zs\le x$ implies $u<x$; so [F2] gives the unshifted decomposition $B_zB_s=B_{zs}\oplus\bigoplus_{u<zs}B_u^{a_u}$, whose summands are perverse by $\mathrm S(zs)$ and $\mathrm S(u)$, while the second term $B_z(1)$ of $B_zF_s=[B_zB_s\to B_z(1)]$ is the internal shift of the perverse $B_z$ sitting in cohomological degree $1$; thus the chosen representative has p-split terms and satisfies $\tau_{<0}(B_zB_s)=0$ and $\tau_{<-1}(B_z(1))=0$, which is membership in $pK^b_{\ge0}$ by [F5].

**Shift propagation.** Assume $\mathrm S(\le x)$ and let $F_x$ be minimal. If $^iF_x$ contains a summand $B_z(j)$ with $z<x$, then $^{i-1}F_x$ contains a summand $B_{z'}(j')$ with $z'>z$ and $j'<j$. First, components of the differential into summands of shift $k<j$ vanish: a degree-zero map $B_z(j)\to B_u(k)$ is an element of $\operatorname{Hom}^{k-j}(B_z,B_u)$, which is zero for $k<j$ since the graded Hom space has no negative-degree part by [F6]; components with $k=j$ are zero for $u\ne z$ by [F6] and are scalars for $u=z$, and a nonzero scalar component would make $B_z(j)$ a contractible summand of the minimal complex, so all such components vanish as well; hence $d(B_z(j))$ lies in the sum of the summands of $^{i+1}F_x$ with shift $k>j$. Second, if a summand $B_u(k)$ of $^{i-1}F_x$ maps nontrivially to $B_z(j)$, then $k<j$: a degree-zero map $B_u(k)\to B_z(j)$ lies in $\operatorname{Hom}^{j-k}(B_u,B_z)$, which vanishes for $j<k$, and for $j=k$ it vanishes for $u\ne z$ and is a scalar for $u=z$, the nonzero case again being excluded by minimality. Third, apply the support cutoff $\Gamma_{\ge z/>z}$ and reduce its free graph modules modulo $R_+$. Since $z<x$, its complex is contractible by [F5], hence this reduced finite-dimensional complex is exact. The chosen top layer $\Delta_z(j)$ of $B_z(j)$ is a nonzero homogeneous basis vector. Every outgoing target has shift $k>j$, and its $z$ layer has shift $k+d$ with $d\ge0$ by KL triangularity. A map from the chosen generator into it consequently has positive-degree coefficient, so vanishes after reduction. The chosen vector is a cycle and must therefore be an incoming boundary. Some incoming component has a nonzero constant coefficient onto it, so some $B_{z'}(j')$ in degree $i-1$ has a $z$ layer with $j'+d=j$. The underlying differential component is nonzero, and the preceding Hom estimate gives $j'<j$. Since $d=0$ for label $z$ itself, this requires $z'>z$. This proves shift propagation without using an Euler identity to recover multiplicities.

**The perverse lower bound for $F_x$.** Use the stupid filtration $w_{\ge k}F_y$ of the minimal complex $F_y$, with distinguished triangles $w_{\ge k+1}F_y\to w_{\ge k}F_y\to{}^kF_y[-k]\to$ and $w_{\ge\ell(y)+1}F_y=0$; tensoring with the invertible $F_s$ preserves distinguished triangles. We prove $(w_{\ge k}F_y)F_s\in pK^b_{\ge0}$ by descending induction on $k$: for $k=\ell(y)+1$ the object is $0$; assume it for $k+1$. By [ih] and step 2.1, $^kF_y$ is a direct sum of summands $B_z(k)$ with $z\le y$ (with $z=y$ only for $k=0$), so $(^kF_y)F_s[-k]$ is a direct sum of copies of $(B_zF_s)(k)[-k]$. Extension closure of $pK^b_{\ge0}$ in the tensored triangles gives $(w_{\ge k}F_y)F_s\in pK^b_{\ge0}$, and at $k=0$ we obtain $F_yF_s\in pK^b_{\ge0}$; by step 2.1 this is $F_x\in pK^b_{\ge0}$.

Now suppose $i\ge1$ and $^iF_x$ has a summand $B_z(k)$ with $k<i$; if $z=x$ this contradicts $m^i_{x,k}=0$ from step 3.2, so $z<x$, and step 4.2 produces a summand $B_{z'}(k')$ of $^{i-1}F_x$ with $k'<k<i$. This summand is again of the forbidden type: if $z'=x$ then $m^{i-1}_{x,k'}=0$ whenever $i-1\ge1$, while for $i-1=0$ it contradicts $^0F_x=B_x$ because $k'<0$; otherwise $z'<x$ and step 4.2 applies again. Iterating this descent in the homological degree we reach a summand of $^0F_x$ with negative internal shift, contradicting $^0F_x=B_x$. Hence every summand of $^iF_x$ has internal shift $\ge i$ for $i\ge1$, which together with $F_x\in pK^b_{\ge0}$ from step 5.1 gives $F_x\in pK^b_{\le0}$; since for $i\ge1$ the label $x$ does not occur by step 3.2, we obtain $^iF_x=\bigoplus_{z<x}B_z(i)^{m_{z,i}}$ with $m_{z,i}:=m^i_{z,i}$, which is (2).

**Inversion of the Kazhdan-Lusztig transition matrix.** Let the two bases be related by $\underline H_w=\sum_{y\le w}h_{y,w}H_y$ and $H_w=\sum_{y\le w}g_{y,w}\underline H_y$ as in [F4]; substituting the first expansion into the second gives $\sum_{y\le z\le w}h_{y,z}g_{z,w}=\delta_{y,w}$. Hence $g_{w,w}=1$ and, for $y<w$, $g_{y,w}=-\sum_{y<z\le w}h_{y,z}g_{z,w}$. We prove $g_{y,w}\in v^{\ell(w)-\ell(y)}\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$ by descending induction on $\ell(w)-\ell(y)$: for $y=w$ this is $1\in v^0\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$, and for $y<w$ each $h_{y,z}$ lies in $v^{\ell(z)-\ell(y)}\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$ by [F4] and each $g_{z,w}$ with $y<z\le w$ lies in $v^{\ell(w)-\ell(z)}\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$ by the hypothesis of the induction, so each product lies in $v^{\ell(w)-\ell(y)}\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$ and the finite sum does too.

**Parity and positivity of the inverse coefficients.** By step 3.2 and step 6.1 the multiplicities appearing in $g_{z,x}=\sum_i(-1)^im_{z,i}v^i$ are exactly the multiplicities of the linear complex $F_x$, and by step 7.1 we have $g_{z,x}\in v^{\ell(x)-\ell(z)}\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$; therefore the coefficient $(-1)^im_{z,i}$ of $v^i$ can be nonzero only when $i\equiv\ell(x)-\ell(z)\pmod2$, which is the parity clause of (3). For such $i$ the sign $(-1)^{\ell(x)-\ell(z)+i}$ equals $+1$, so $(-1)^{\ell(x)-\ell(z)}g_{z,x}=\sum_i(-1)^{\ell(x)-\ell(z)+i}m_{z,i}v^i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}[v^{\pm1}]$, and the coefficients are the nonnegative multiplicities $m_{z,i}$. This proves (3) and, with (1) and (2), completes the induction.

boundaries.evidence: The empty word is the base of the induction and is discharged at the start of step 1.1: the complex is the unit in degree zero, there are no higher terms, both perverse bounds are trivial and the multiplicity statement is vacuous.

The degree-zero term is pinned down in step 6.1: a lower summand there would propagate to a summand of the term in degree -1, which is zero, so the top term is exactly the indecomposable; the vanishing of the negative terms is what drives the argument.

The unit-length word is the first nontrivial instance of the induction: step 2.1 sets up the last letter with the induction hypothesis for the shorter word, and step 3.1 handles the descent contraction used when that letter lowers the length.

Non-reduced or non-minimal representatives are excluded by the hypotheses rather than assumed away: step 5.1 splits off the contractible summand of the perverse truncation and step 3.1 performs the descent contraction only across an invertible differential block.

The two perverse bounds are the grading endpoints: step 4.1 proves the lower bound for the ascent complex, step 6.1 the upper bound, and linearity pins each summand of the degree-indexed term at exactly the matching internal shift.
Choice-free: the induction runs over the finite set of permutations, and every cancellation in steps 3.1 and 5.1 is performed on an explicitly invertible block.

boundaries.reason: The theorem is a list of structural conclusions about a minimal complex; it states no equivalence, so there is no forward direction to discharge.
No converse is claimed: the linearity and multiplicity statements are proved directly from the character hypotheses, not as one side of a biconditional.

type-$A$ block with $W=S_n$, and for $w\in W$ let $B_{w^{-1}}$ be the polynomial
Soergel lift of $V(P(w\cdot\lambda))$, so that
$V(P(w\cdot\lambda))=\bar B_{w^{-1}}$ is its right reduction. Write
$r_{x,d}(B)$ for the graded multiplicity of the polynomial standard graph
module supported at $x$ in the standard support filtration of a polynomial
Soergel bimodule $B$, in the standard-generator normalization of the polynomial
Soergel category. Then for all $y,w\in W$
$$(P(w\cdot\lambda):\Delta(y\cdot\lambda))=\sum_d r_{y^{-1},d}(B_{w^{-1}}).$$
These are ranks before reduction: the right side sums the graded standard
support multiplicities of the polynomial lift, not multiplicities in any
separated filtration of the finite-dimensional module $V(P(w\cdot\lambda))$.

**Graphs and supports.** Keep $k=\mathbb Q$, $R=\mathbb Q[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ with
$\deg x_i=2$, and the affine scheme $V=\mathbb A^n_k=\operatorname{Spec}R$,
whose $k$-points are $V(k)=k^n$. Use the place-permuting action of $S_n$
from [[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]].
For $w\in S_n$ let
$$Gr(w):=\operatorname{Graph}(w:V\to V)\subseteq V\times_kV,\quad Gr(w)(k)=\{(w\lambda,\lambda):\lambda\in k^n\},\qquad Gr(A):=\bigcup_{w\in A}Gr(w)\ \ (A\subseteq S_n),$$
so that $V\times_kV=\operatorname{Spec}(R\otimes_kR)$ and $Gr(w)$ is the graph
of the map $\lambda\mapsto w\lambda$. A graded $(R,R)$-bimodule $M$ is the
same thing as a graded module over $R\otimes_kR$, and the support of $m\in M$ is
the zero set $\operatorname{supp}(m):=V(\operatorname{Ann}(m))\subseteq V\times V$
of its annihilator ideal in $R\otimes_kR$. For $A\subseteq S_n$ put
$$\Gamma_AM:=\{m\in M:\operatorname{supp}(m)\subseteq Gr(A)\},$$
a graded sub-bimodule of $M$. Since $Gr(A)$ is closed with radical ideal
$I(Gr(A))=\bigcap_{w\in A}I(Gr(w))$ (an intersection of prime ideals, since each
$Gr(w)$ is a linear subspace of $V\times V$ complementing the second factor), an
element $m$ lies in $\Gamma_AM$ exactly when $I(Gr(A))^N m=0$ for some $N\ge0$:
this is the Nullstellensatz together with the Noetherianity of
$R\otimes_kR$. The ideal itself need not annihilate such an element — in
$(R\otimes_kR)/I(Gr(e))^2$ the class of $1$ is supported on $Gr(e)$ but is not
killed by $I(Gr(e))$ — which is why the criterion is stated with a power of the
ideal. For $i\in\mathbb Z$ we write
$$\Gamma_{\ge i}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\ell(x)\ge i\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{\le i}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\ell(x)\le i\}}M,$$
using the length function of [[lem-type-a-reduced-words-are-connected-by-braid-moves]],
while for $y\in S_n$ the $y$-indexed symbols denote the *Bruhat
principal-set* cutoffs of Soergel's Notation 6.1,
$$\Gamma_{\le y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x\le y\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{<y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x<y\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{\ge y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x\ge y\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{>y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x>y\}}M,$$
with $\Gamma_yM:=\Gamma_{\{y\}}M$ the elements concentrated on the single graph
$Gr(y)$ and $\Gamma_{\ne y}M:=\Gamma_{S_n\setminus\{y\}}M$ the elements
concentrated off $Gr(y)$. The integer-indexed symbols of the previous display are
the *length* cutoffs used to define the flags below, and they must not be
confused with the element-indexed Bruhat cutoffs: for $y=s_1$ in $S_4$ the
submodule $\Gamma_{\le1}M$ contains $Gr(s_3)$ while
$\Gamma_{\le y}M=\Gamma_{\{e,s_1\}}M$ does not, and the two cutoffs agree at
the extremes, $\Gamma_{\le w_0}=\Gamma_{\le\ell(w_0)}=M$ and
$\Gamma_{<e}=\Gamma_{\le-1}=0$. So
$\Gamma^yM:=M/\Gamma_{\ne y}M$ is Soergel's $y$-layer
*quotient*; following Soergel's
Notation 6.1 we write the two $y$-layer quotients with an underline,
$$\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M:=\Gamma_{\le y}M/\Gamma_{<y}M,\qquad \underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M:=\Gamma_{\ge y}M/\Gamma_{>y}M,$$
so that $\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M$ is the quotient of the lower support
submodule by $\Gamma_{<y}M$ and $\underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M$ the quotient of
the upper support submodule by the part supported strictly above $Gr(y)$.

which equals $R$ as a graded $k$-vector space and has
$$f\cdot x=fx,\qquad x\cdot g=w(g)\,x\qquad(f,g,x\in R),$$

[[def-graded-ring-module-bimodule-and-internal-shift]], so that
$M(k)_d=M_{d+k}$; this is the shift convention of the type-A sources, and it is
the one in which $B_i=R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R(1)$ of
[[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]] has $1\otimes1$ of
degree $-1$. Put
$$\Delta_w(d):=R_w(d-\ell(w)),\qquad \nabla_w(d):=R_w(d+\ell(w))\qquad(d\in\mathbb Z),$$
so that $\Delta_w(d)$ is the standard bimodule $R_w$ with its generator in
degree $\ell(w)-d$, and $\nabla_w(d)$ is $R_w$ with its generator in degree
$-\ell(w)-d$. Thus $\Delta_w(0)=R_w\{\ell(w)\}$,
$\nabla_w(0)=R_w\{-\ell(w)\}$ and $\Delta_e(d)=\nabla_e(d)=R(d)$ is generated

For graded free $R$-modules in this type-A page, a homogeneous free generator of degree $a$ contributes $v^a$ to graded rank. This is the $v\mapsto v^{-1}$ transform of Soergel's rank convention in his Notation 5.2; all rank formulas below use this convention.

finite chain $0=M_0\subseteq M_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq M_k=M$ of graded
sub-bimodules which refines the length filtration
$$M=\Gamma_{\ge0}M\supseteq\Gamma_{\ge1}M\supseteq\cdots\supseteq\Gamma_{\ge\ell(w_0)+1}M=0$$
of $M$ (here $\Gamma_{\ge0}M=M$ for every bimodule supported on
$Gr(S_n)=\bigcup_{w}Gr(w)$, which all bimodules of this page are, and
$\Gamma_{\ge i}M=0$ for $i>\ell(w_0)$ because no graph $Gr(x)$ with
$\ell(x)>i$ remains) and whose successive quotients are
standard bimodules $M_j/M_{j-1}\cong R_{x_j}\{a_j\}$. We require each
length layer to be a finite direct sum of shifted graph bimodules of that
length, as in Soergel's Definition 5.4. Thus the
quotients carry a numbering with $\ell(x_1)\ge\cdots\ge\ell(x_k)$ and each
$R_{x_j}\{a_j\}$ is one graph, so that $M$ has a "support flag" in the sense of
Soergel's $F_\Delta$. A $\nabla$-flag has the same direct-sum condition on its length layers, with the reverse length
filtration $\Gamma_{\le i}M$ and $\ell(x_1)\le\cdots\le\ell(x_k)$. The
refinement condition is a condition on supports, not an ordering of incomparable
quotients of equal length; only the lengths are ordered. For $i=\ell(x)$ the
graded multiplicity is

$\nabla_x(d)$ in $\Gamma_{\le i}M/\Gamma_{\le i-1}M$; a priori both symbols

[[lem-type-a-hecke-standard-basis-for-soergel-comparison]] and

$$h_\Delta(M):=\sum_{x,d}(M:\Delta_x(d))\,v^d\,\widetilde T_x,\qquad h_\nabla(M):=\sum_{x,d}(M:\nabla_x(d))\,v^{-d}\,\widetilde T_x,$$
and they are used only through the items that prove these sums intrinsic.

([[def-split-grothendieck-rings-of-type-a-soergel-categories]]) and let
$h_\Delta,h_\nabla$ be the intrinsic $\Delta$- and $\nabla$-multiplicity
characters of
[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]],
which by [[lem-type-a-support-filtration-multiplicities-are-intrinsic]] are
well-defined functions of the bimodule and additive on direct sums, so that
they descend to $\mathbb Z$-linear maps on $K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(\mathrm{SBim}_n)$
with values in the Hecke algebra $H_{S_n}$ of
[[def-type-a-hecke-algebra-in-soergel-normalization]] whose normalized
generators are $H_i=v(T_i+1)$. Then:

   $$h_\Delta:K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(\mathrm{SBim}_n)\longrightarrow H_{S_n},\qquad h_\Delta(XY)=h_\Delta(X)h_\Delta(Y),\qquad h_\Delta(vX)=v\,h_\Delta(X),$$ that is
   $h_\Delta(vX)=v\,h_\Delta(X)$, and $h_\Delta([B_i])=H_i$ for every simple
   reflection;
2. $h_\nabla$ is multiplicative, $h_\nabla(XY)=h_\nabla(X)h_\nabla(Y)$, and

multiplicity forces the index direction, i.e.

order. The first sense is the inclusion direction of
[[lem-dominant-integral-dot-translates-embed-in-the-verma-module]] (for

confines every composition factor of $M(y\cdot\lambda)$ to labels
$w\ge y$. The full statement that the two orders are isomorphic as posets is
not needed here and is not asserted; only these two directions, together with

([[lem-bruhat-order-basic-properties-for-permutations]]), are used.

symmetry $p_{y^{-1},w^{-1}}=p_{y,w}$.

polynomial standard graph bimodule supported at $x$, and $B_x$ for the
normalized indecomposable polynomial Soergel bimodule, which is generally not a
standard graph bimodule. With right reduction $\bar B=B\otimes_S\mathbb C$
and left coinvariant-module values of $V$, the projective dictionary is

([[thm-indecomposable-projectives-correspond-to-indecomposable-soergel-modules]]).
The graph label $x$ corresponds to the standard
$\Delta(x^{-1}\cdot\lambda)$. The individual support ranks are measured on the
polynomial lift before reduction, as in
[[prop-verma-flag-multiplicities-are-standard-filtration-ranks-under-v]];

[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]]:

One writes $\mu(y|w)
e0$ when $y
e w$ and ($y<w$ and $\mu(y,w)
e0$) or ($w<y$ and $\mu(w,y)
e0$). The dictionary with the literature is recorded for use: with the classical parameter $T_s^2=(q-1)T_s+q$ one has $H_w=v^{\ell(w)}T_w$, the element $\underline H_w$ is the basis element $C'_w$ of [EW], and $h_{y,w}=p_{y,w}$ with $v^{\ell(w)-\ell(y)}P_{y,w}(v^{-2})=h_{y,w}$ [EW, Remark 3.2].
