derivations.claim: The comparison of [F1] expresses the Verma-flag multiplicity of the indecomposable projective $P(w\cdot\lambda)$ as the total graded standard-support rank of the polynomial lift $B_{w^{-1}}$: $(P(w\cdot\lambda):\Delta(y\cdot\lambda))=\sum_d r_{y^{-1},d}(B_{w^{-1}})$.

The character theorem [F2] gives $h_\Delta(B_{w^{-1}})=\underline H_{w^{-1}}=\sum_xp_{x,w^{-1}}H_x$. By the coefficient formula of [F3], the left side is $\sum_xm_x(B_{w^{-1}};v)H_x$, where $m_x(B_{w^{-1}};v)=\sum_dr_{x,d}(B_{w^{-1}})v^d$ uses the normalized polynomial standard layers before reduction. Comparing coefficients in the standard Hecke basis of [F4] yields $m_x(B_{w^{-1}};v)=p_{x,w^{-1}}(v)$ for every $x$, as an identity of Laurent polynomials. This comparison uses the character formula; it does not identify an indecomposable class with a product of simple classes.

Evaluate step 1.2 at the label $x=y^{-1}$ and at $v=1$: the left side becomes $\sum_d r_{y^{-1},d}(B_{w^{-1}})$, which equals the multiplicity by step 1.1, and the right side becomes $p_{y^{-1},w^{-1}}(1)$; the inversion symmetry $p_{y^{-1},w^{-1}}=p_{y,w}$ of [F4] and the specialization $p_{y,w}(1)=P_{y,w}(1)$ of [F5] turn this into $(P(w\cdot\lambda):\Delta(y\cdot\lambda))=P_{y,w}(1)$ for all $y,w\in W$. The vanishing clause is the support statement $p_{y,w}=0$ unless $y\le w$ of [F4] and [F5], and only the total value at one is used: no individual coefficient of $P_{y,w}$ is interpreted as a category-$\mathcal O$ multiplicity, and no grading on $\mathcal O$ is constructed — the grading in play is the auxiliary grading of the polynomial lift, normalized on the Soergel side.

boundaries.evidence: Step 2.1 evaluates the identity at the label x = y^{-1}; when y is not below w the support clause p_{y,w} = 0 makes both sides the empty-sum value 0, which is the stated vanishing.
Zero multiplicities are an instance of the displayed equality in step 2.1, not an exception: for incomparable pairs the theorem asserts (P(w.lambda):Delta(y.lambda)) = P_{y,w}(1) = 0.
The diagonal case y = w is included: [F4] fixes p_{w,w} = 1 and the step 2.1 evaluation gives multiplicity P_{w,w}(1) = 1 at the unit label.

boundaries.reason: The Theorem is stated only for regular integral type-A blocks; singular or non-integral blocks are excluded by its hypothesis and are handled on other pages.

boundaries.evidence: The endpoint labels are included in step 2.1's quantifier: at y = e the support condition is automatic for every w, and at w = e the sum collapses to the diagonal term.
The Statement assumes AC; step 1.1 consumes it only through the rank comparison [F1], whose choice content is inherited from the block and projective theory.

boundaries.reason: The Theorem is an equality of two multiplicities; its only directional content is the support statement already disposed as the zero case, and no implication requires a separate discharge.
No converse is asserted. The Theorem does not claim that the value P_{y,w}(1) computes anything outside the regular integral block regime.

$\mathcal O_\lambda$, for all $y,w\in W$
$$(P(w\cdot\lambda):\Delta(y\cdot\lambda))=P_{y,w}(1),$$
the value at $q=1$ of the classical Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomial of the pair
$y\le w$; the multiplicity is the total value at one, not an individual
coefficient of $P_{y,w}$, and it vanishes unless $y\le w$ in the Bruhat order.

Fix a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ of type
$A_{n-1}$ with Cartan $\mathfrak h$, positive system $\Phi^+$, Weyl vector
$\rho$, Weyl group $W$ (identified with $S_n$) and dot action
$w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$. Fix a dominant regular integral weight
$\lambda$, i.e. $\langle\lambda+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle\neq0$ for every root and
$\lambda$ integral, and let $\mathcal O_\lambda$ be the corresponding regular
integral block in the conventions of
[[def-regular-integral-category-o-block-and-its-antidominant-weight]]: standard
objects $\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)=M(w\cdot\lambda)$, simples $L(w\cdot\lambda)$,
indecomposable projectives $P(w\cdot\lambda)$ for $w\in W$, with
$\lambda=e\cdot\lambda$ the unique dominant and $w_0\cdot\lambda$ the unique
antidominant element and $\Delta(w_0\cdot\lambda)=L(w_0\cdot\lambda)$.

This item freezes the following conventions, each inherited from the cited
suppliers and used verbatim below.

(i) **Multiplicity conventions.** $(P(w\cdot\lambda):\Delta(y\cdot\lambda))$ is
the Verma-flag multiplicity of [[def-verma-flag-and-its-multiplicities]] and
$[M(y\cdot\lambda):L(w\cdot\lambda)]$ the composition multiplicity, and
$$(P(w\cdot\lambda):\Delta(y\cdot\lambda))=[M(y\cdot\lambda):L(w\cdot\lambda)]$$
by BGG reciprocity ([[thm-bgg-reciprocity]]).

(ii) **Bruhat reversal convention.** Along the bijection
$W\ni w\mapsto w\cdot\lambda$ the Bruhat order runs opposite to the dominance
order, in the two exact senses used on this page: $y\le w$ implies
$w\cdot\lambda\le y\cdot\lambda$ in the dominance order, and every nonzero
multiplicity forces the index direction, i.e.
$[M(y\cdot\lambda):L(w\cdot\lambda)]\neq0$ implies $y\le w$ in the Bruhat
order. The first sense is the inclusion direction of
[[lem-dominant-integral-dot-translates-embed-in-the-verma-module]] (for
$w\ge y$ one has $M(w\cdot\lambda)\subseteq M(y\cdot\lambda)$, so the highest
weight of the submodule is the lower one), and the second is
[[lem-jordan-holder-factors-of-verma-modules-lie-above-the-head]], which
confines every composition factor of $M(y\cdot\lambda)$ to labels
$w\ge y$. The full statement that the two orders are isomorphic as posets is
not needed here and is not asserted; only these two directions, together with
the finiteness of intervals of the Bruhat order
([[lem-bruhat-order-basic-properties-for-permutations]]), are used.

(iii) **Hecke and Kazhdan–Lusztig normalization.** The Kazhdan–Lusztig basis
$\underline H_w=\sum_{y\le w}p_{y,w}H_y$ of the normalized type-$A$ Hecke
algebra ([[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-the-kazhdan-lusztig-basis]]), with
$$p_{y,w}=v^{\ell(w)-\ell(y)}P_{y,w}(v^{-2})$$
in the classical $q=v^{-2}$ normalization
([[def-kazhdan-lusztig-polynomials-in-the-classical-q-normalization]]), support
$p_{y,w}=0$ unless $y\le w$, diagonal $p_{w,w}=1$, and simultaneous inversion
symmetry $p_{y^{-1},w^{-1}}=p_{y,w}$.

(iv) **Soergel label and character dictionary.** Write $R_x$ for the
polynomial standard graph bimodule supported at $x$, and $B_x$ for the
normalized indecomposable polynomial Soergel bimodule, which is generally not a
standard graph bimodule. With right reduction $\bar B=B\otimes_S\mathbb C$
and left coinvariant-module values of $V$, the projective dictionary is
$$V(P(w\cdot\lambda))\cong\bar B_{w^{-1}}$$
([[thm-indecomposable-projectives-correspond-to-indecomposable-soergel-modules]]).
The graph label $x$ corresponds to the standard
$\Delta(x^{-1}\cdot\lambda)$. The individual support ranks are measured on the
polynomial lift before reduction, as in
[[prop-verma-flag-multiplicities-are-standard-filtration-ranks-under-v]];
no separated graph-support filtration of the reduced module is asserted.

For degree bookkeeping use precisely the standard-generator normalization of
[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]]:
$\Delta_x(d)=R_x(d-\ell(x))$, and $r_{x,d}(B)$ counts these normalized polynomial
standard layers. Thus the coefficient polynomial is
$$m_x(B;v):=\sum_d r_{x,d}(B)v^d,\qquad h_\Delta(B)=\sum_xm_x(B;v)\widetilde T_x,\qquad\widetilde T_x=v^{\ell(x)}T_x.$$
Here $\widetilde T_x$ is the normalized **standard** Hecke element $H_x$ used
in clause (iii) and
[[def-normalized-type-a-hecke-algebra-and-its-bar-involution]]. The published
Soergel split-Grothendieck-ring convention instead names its simple
Kazhdan--Lusztig generators $H_i=v(T_i+1)=\widetilde T_{s_i}+v$; these must not
be confused with the standard element $H_{s_i}=vT_i$
([[thm-split-grothendieck-group-of-the-soergel-category-is-the-type-a-hecke-algebra]]).
The standard-character supplier
[[lem-the-type-a-standard-character-is-multiplicative]] identifies $h_\Delta$
with that split-Grothendieck-ring isomorphism. This records the coefficient
normalization, and does not infer the image of a general indecomposable $B_x$
by multiplying simple generators. In particular the character theorem must be
used to identify $h_\Delta(B_x)$ with $\underline H_x$; a product of simple
Soergel classes is a Bott--Samelson class and need not be $[B_x]$.
The inverse labels and all rank comparisons above use auxiliary polynomial
gradings only; forgetting them gives the ordinary projective dictionary.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Work in category
$\mathcal O$ with the conventions of [[def-bgg-category-o]], and write
$\Delta(\mu)=M(\mu)$ for the standard objects of
[[def-standard-and-costandard-objects-in-category-o]], i.e. the Verma modules
of [[def-verma-module]].

A **finite Verma flag** of an object $X$ of $\mathcal O$ — also called a
**standard flag** or a **$\Delta$-flag** — is a finite increasing sequence of
subobjects
$$0=X_0\subseteq X_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq X_n=X$$
such that each quotient $X_i/X_{i-1}$ is isomorphic to a Verma module
$\Delta(\mu_i)=M(\mu_i)$, for $i=1,\dots,n$. An object admitting such a flag is
called **Verma-filtered**. Since the flag is exhausted by its factors, its
class in the Grothendieck group
$K_0(\mathcal O)$ of [[def-grothendieck-group-and-character-of-category-o]]
is
$$[X]=\sum_{i=1}^n[\Delta(\mu_i)].$$

For a Verma-filtered object $X$ and a weight $\mu$, the **multiplicity**
$(X:\Delta(\mu))$ is the number of indices $i$ with $\mu_i=\mu$ in a Verma
flag of $X$. This number is independent of the chosen flag by
[[lem-verma-flag-multiplicities-are-independent-of-the-flag]], so the notation
$(X:\Delta(\mu))$ is well-defined for Verma-filtered $X$.

The zero object has the empty flag, and every multiplicity of the zero object
is zero; a nonzero Verma-filtered object has at least one factor. A one-step
flag of $X$ is exactly an isomorphism $X\cong\Delta(\mu)$ for a single weight
$\mu$, so the objects with a one-step flag are the Verma modules themselves.
The flag is a chain of subobjects of $X$ in the module category; it is not
required to split, and later examples show that it need not.

Identify $\mathbb Z[q]$ with $\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$ by $q\mapsto v^{-2}$. For $y\le w$ in $S_n$, put $d=\ell(w)-\ell(y)$ and define the **Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomial** $P_{y,w}(q)\in\mathbb Z[q]$ by $$P_{y,w}(v^{-2})=v^{-d}p_{y,w},$$ where $\underline H_w=\sum_{y\le w}p_{y,w}H_y$ is the Kazhdan–Lusztig basis of [[lem-type-a-kazhdan-lusztig-basis-has-elementary-triangular-bar-properties]]. The parity clause of that theorem makes the right side a polynomial in $v^{-2}$. The conventions are: $P_{y,w}=0$ unless $y\le w$, $P_{w,w}=1$, $P_{y,w}$ has constant term 1, and for $y<w$ its degree is at most $(\ell(w)-\ell(y)-1)/2$. The **$\mu$-coefficient** is $$\mu(y,w):=	ext{coefficient of }q^{(\ell(w)-\ell(y)-1)/2}	ext{ in }P_{y,w},$$ defined to be 0 when $\ell(w)-\ell(y)$ is even; equivalently $\mu(y,w)$ is the coefficient of $v$ in $p_{y,w}$. One writes $\mu(y|w)
e0$ when $y
e w$ and ($y<w$ and $\mu(y,w)
e0$) or ($w<y$ and $\mu(w,y)
e0$). The dictionary with the literature is recorded for use: with the classical parameter $T_s^2=(q-1)T_s+q$ one has $H_w=v^{\ell(w)}T_w$, the element $\underline H_w$ is the basis element $C'_w$ of [EW], and $h_{y,w}=p_{y,w}$ with $v^{\ell(w)-\ell(y)}P_{y,w}(v^{-2})=h_{y,w}$ [EW, Remark 3.2].

Let $s=s_i$ be a simple reflection, $w\in S_n$ with $sw<w$, and $y\le w$. With $P_{x,z}:=0$ whenever $x\not\le z$, $$P_{y,w}(q)=q^{1-c}P_{sy,sw}(q)+q^{c}P_{y,sw}(q)-\!\!\!\sum_{\substack{y\le z\le sw\\ sz<z,\ \mu(z,sw)\ne0}}\!\!\!\mu(z,sw)\,q^{(\ell(w)-\ell(z))/2}P_{y,z}(q),$$ where $c=1$ if $sy<y$ and $c=0$ if $sy>y$; here $\mu$ is the coefficient defined in [[def-kazhdan-lusztig-polynomials-in-the-classical-q-normalization]] (so the summand only occurs for $\ell(sw)-\ell(z)$ odd, and $(\ell(w)-\ell(z))/2$ is then an integer). The same recursion holds with $s\in R(w)$ (right descents) after replacing each index $x$ by $x^{-1}$, using $P_{y^{-1},w^{-1}}=P_{y,w}$ and $\mu(y^{-1},w^{-1})=\mu(y,w)$.

Let $\le$ be the rank-inequality order on the zero-based $S_n$ of [[def-bruhat-order-on-the-symmetric-group]], and identify it with the one-based realization by shifting inputs and values by $1$. (a) This order is the strong Bruhat order of type A: the transitive closure of covers $x\to tx$ where $t$ is a transposition and $\ell(tx)=\ell(x)+1$. (b) If $y\le w$ then $\ell(y)\le\ell(w)$, with equality iff $y=w$; every saturated chain has $\ell(w)-\ell(y)$ steps; and $y\le w$ iff $y^{-1}\le w^{-1}$. (c) $y\le w$ iff for every reduced expression $w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k}$, $y$ is a reduced subword. (d) For every simple reflection $s$, if $y\le w$ and $\ell(sy)>\ell(y)$, then $y\le sw$; if $y\le w$ and $\ell(sw)<\ell(w)$, then $sy\le w$. (e) Every interval $[y,w]$ is finite; if $y\le w$, then $[y,w]=\{y\}\cup\bigcup_{y\to a\le w}[a,w]$.

Let $n\ge1$ and $y,w\in S_n$. The **Bruhat interval** $[y,w]:=\{z\in S_n:y\le z\le w\}$ is finite, with Bruhat order as in [[lem-bruhat-order-basic-properties-for-permutations]] and [[def-bruhat-order-on-the-symmetric-group]]. The rank-order definition uses the zero-based model of $S_n$, while $H_v(n)$ uses the one-based model; throughout, identify them by the order-preserving shift $i\mapsto i+1$ on inputs and values.

The **$R$-coefficients** $r_{y,w}\in A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ are the unique coefficients in the standard-basis expansion
$$\overline{H_w}=H_{w^{-1}}^{-1}=\sum_{y\in S_n}r_{y,w}H_y,$$
where the bar is the involution from [[lem-the-hecke-bar-involution-is-well-defined]] and $\{H_y:y\in S_n\}$ is the standard basis of [[def-normalized-type-a-hecke-algebra-and-its-bar-involution]]. The sum has finite support because $S_n$ is finite. In rank one, $\overline{H_{s_i}}=H_{s_i}^{-1}=H_{s_i}+(v-v^{-1})H_{\mathrm{id}}$, so $r_{\mathrm{id},s_i}=v-v^{-1}$.

The support, diagonal, and parity properties of these coefficients are stated and proved in [[thm-r-polynomial-recursion-and-degree-bounds]]. This page uses the coefficient normalization given by the displayed bar expansion.

derivations.claim: **The interval.** The word $s_2s_1s_3s_2$ has length $4$ and is reduced, since $3412$ has exactly the four inversions $(3,1),(3,2),(4,1),(4,2)$. Its reduced subwords give: $1234$ at length $0$; $2134,1324,1243$ at length $1$; $1342,1423,2314,3124,2143$ at length $2$; $1432,2413,3142,3214$ at length $3$; and $3412$ at length $4$. The four elements $1234,2134,1243,2143$ contain no reduced subword equal to $s_2=1324$, so they are not above $b$ by the reduced-subword criterion; the remaining ten elements are exactly $[b,w]$.

**All gaps at most two have $P=1$.** Suppose $y<z$ and $d:=\ell(z)-\ell(y)\le2$. By [F3] the degree of $P_{y,z}$ is at most $(d-1)/2\le1/2$, hence at most $0$; together with constant term $1$ this forces $P_{y,z}=1$. If $d=0$ then $y=z$ and $P_{y,y}=1$; if $y$ and $z$ are incomparable, $P_{y,z}=0$ by [F3]. In particular $P_{b,2413}=1$ and $P_{1234,1423}=1$, both pairs having gap $2$.

**The recursion at $(\mathrm{id},2413)$.** Write $\mathrm{id}=1234$ and use $2413=s_1s_3s_2$, a reduced word with left descent $s_1$. With $s=s_1$ one has $s\,2413=1423$ and $s\,\mathrm{id}=2134$, so $c=0$ in [F4] and $$P_{\mathrm{id},2413}(q)=q\,P_{2134,1423}(q)+P_{\mathrm{id},1423}(q)-\!\!\!\sum_{\substack{\mathrm{id}\le u\le1423\\ s_1u<u,\ \mu(u,1423)\ne0}}\!\!\!\mu(u,1423)\,q^{(3-\ell(u))/2}P_{\mathrm{id},u}(q).$$ The first summand vanishes: $1423=s_3s_2$ has no reduced subword $s_1$, so $2134\not\le1423$ and $P_{2134,1423}=0$ by [F3] and [F5]. The correction sum is empty as well: $[\mathrm{id},1423]=\{1234,1324,1243,1423\}$ by step 1.1, and for each of these four elements left multiplication by $s_1$ swaps the values $1$ and $2$, raising the length from $0,1,1,2$ to $1,2,2,3$ respectively, so no element of the interval has the required left descent $s_1$. By step 1.2 the remaining term is $P_{\mathrm{id},1423}=1$, hence $P_{\mathrm{id},2413}=1$.

**The main recursion.** Apply [F4] to $b=1324$, $w=3412$ and the left descent $s=s_2$: $s_2w=2413$ and $s_2b=1234$, so $c=1$ because $s_2b$ has length $0<1=\ell(b)$, and $$P_{b,w}(q)=P_{\mathrm{id},2413}(q)+q\,P_{b,2413}(q)-\!\!\!\sum_{\substack{b\le u\le2413\\ s_2u<u,\ \mu(u,2413)\ne0}}\!\!\!\mu(u,2413)\,q^{(4-\ell(u))/2}P_{b,u}(q).$$ By step 1.1 the interval $[b,2413]$ is $\{1324,1423,2314,2413\}$; left multiplication by $s_2$ swaps the values $2$ and $3$, turning these into $1234,1432,3214,3412$ of lengths $0,3,3,4$, so only $u=b$ has the required descent, and there $\mu(b,2413)=0$ because $\ell(2413)-\ell(b)=2$ is even by [F3]. The correction sum is therefore empty; step 2.1 gives $P_{\mathrm{id},2413}=1$ and step 1.2 gives $P_{b,2413}=1$, so $P_{b,w}=1+q$, with $\mu(b,w)=1$ and $\ell(w)-\ell(b)=3$.

**The comparison.** The polynomial $P_{b,w}(q)=1+q$ has leading coefficient $1$ (the coefficient of $q^{1}$, its degree being $1$) while its value at $q=1$ is $2$. The multiplicity theorem [F1] computes the ordinary Verma-flag multiplicity as $(P(w\cdot\lambda):\Delta(b\cdot\lambda))=P_{b,w}(1)=2$, with $0$ dominant regular integral in $\mathfrak{sl}_4$ (indeed $\langle\rho,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle=1\ne0$ for every simple root and $0$ is integral). Hence the leading coefficient $1$ of the Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomial differs from the multiplicity $2$: the refuted claim's coefficientwise clause is false, and neither individual coefficient of this polynomial equals the ordinary multiplicity; its total value at one does. This is a genuine failure of the claim and not an artefact of undefined quantities: $b\le w$, all polynomials are classical Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials, and the multiplicity is that of the ordinary block $\mathcal O_0$.

**The grading clause.** The remaining structural clause of the refuted claim is not supplied by the cited results either: the multiplicity of [F1] is the ordinary (ungraded) Verma-flag multiplicity, and the projective dictionary of [F2] is the ungraded reduction $V(P(w\cdot\lambda))=\bar B_{w^{-1}}$, whose auxiliary grading lives on the polynomial lift and is not a grading of $\mathcal O_\lambda$. Thus the character identity at $q=1$ cannot establish that the block is graded or Koszul; the graded and $\mathrm{Ext}$ refinements belong to the separate Koszul-duality frontier, and step 4.1 refutes only the identification of an individual coefficient with an ordinary multiplicity. It does not refute graded decomposition numbers or the possibility of a Koszul grading: those require additional constructions and proofs, and graded multiplicities may sum to the ordinary multiplicity. The stated conjunction is refuted by its false leading-coefficient clause, with witness $(y,w)=(1324,3412)$ in $\mathfrak{sl}_4$.

Step 4.1 compares each individual coefficient 1 of 1+q with the ordinary multiplicity 2. Step 5.1 explicitly limits the refutation to ordinary multiplicities and does not refute graded decomposition numbers or Koszulity.

Step 4.1 verifies the witness is non-degenerate: b <= w is a genuine comparable pair of gap 3 in a regular integral block of sl_4, so the failure is not an artefact of undefined or excluded quantities.

The witness is the endpoint pair (1324,3412) of its interval; step 1.2 shows every gap <= 2 pair has P = 1, so the endpoint is the unique place the refuted coefficientwise reading could fail and it does.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. In a regular integral type-$A$ block
$\mathcal O_\lambda$, for all $y,w\in W$
$$[M(y\cdot\lambda):L(w\cdot\lambda)]=(P(w\cdot\lambda):\Delta(y\cdot\lambda))=P_{y,w}(1),$$
with the pair ordered so that the multiplicity vanishes unless $y\le w$ in the
Bruhat order; in particular the Kazhdan–Lusztig conjecture's multiplicity
statement holds for every dominant regular integral weight, with the same
combinatorial answer.

Assume the Axiom of Choice.

Fix a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, and a positive Borel $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$. Write $Q^+=\sum_i\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\alpha_i$, $\mu\leq\lambda$ when $\lambda-\mu\in Q^+$, and $w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$.

The classes $[L(\lambda)]$, and separately the classes $[M(\lambda)]$, form $\mathbb Z$-bases of $K_0(\mathcal O)$. For a fixed finite central-character label set $\Lambda=W\cdot\lambda$, the transition between its standard and simple classes is unitriangular in any linear order extending $\leq$. This remains true on a downward-closed subset of that finite poset. It is not a claim about finite downward ideals of all of $\mathfrak h^*$.

Fix a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, and a positive Borel $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$. Write $Q^+=\sum_i\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\alpha_i$, $\mu\leq\lambda$ when $\lambda-\mu\in Q^+$, and $w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$.

For the abelian category [[thm-category-o-is-abelian-and-extension-closed]], define $K_0(\mathcal O)$ as the free abelian group on isomorphism classes $[M]$, modulo $[B]=[A]+[C]$ for every short exact sequence $0\to A\to B\to C\to0$. A set of representatives suffices: every finitely generated $U(\mathfrak g)$-module is a quotient of some $U(\mathfrak g)^n$, and those quotients form a set up to isomorphism.

Define the formal character by $\operatorname{ch}M=\sum_\mu(\dim M_\mu)e^\mu$. By [[prop-equivalent-support-description-of-category-o]], its integer coefficients are finite and supported in finitely many downward cones. Let $\mathscr R$ be the group of all such integer coefficient families, with pointwise addition. It is a ring with $e^\mu e^\nu=e^{\mu+\nu}$: at a fixed resulting weight, in any pair of cones the equation $\beta+\gamma=\eta$ with $\beta,\gamma\in Q^+$ has finitely many solutions, since every simple-root coefficient is bounded. Taking weight spaces is exact, so character gives a well-defined homomorphism $K_0(\mathcal O)\to\mathscr R$. The zero object's class and character are zero.

For $x,w\in S_n$ set $$q'_{x,w}:=\sum_{m\ge0}(-1)^m\sum_{x=z_0<z_1<\cdots<z_m=w}p_{z_0,z_1}p_{z_1,z_2}\cdots p_{z_{m-1},z_m}\in A,$$ where the inner sum is over strictly increasing Bruhat chains from $x$ to $w$, the $m=0$ chain occurs only when $x=w$, and $p_{u,v}$ are the coefficients of the Kazhdan–Lusztig basis ([[lem-type-a-kazhdan-lusztig-basis-has-elementary-triangular-bar-properties]]). Every chain lies in a finite Bruhat interval by [[lem-bruhat-order-basic-properties-for-permutations]], so the sum is finite. If $x\not\le w$ there are no chains; if $x=w$, the empty chain gives $q'_{w,w}=1$. If $x<w$, each chain has at least one factor $p_{u,v}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ with $u<v$, so $q'_{x,w}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$.

Let $P=(p_{x,w})$ and $Q'=(q'_{x,w})$. The matrix $N:=P-I$ is strictly triangular on the finite Bruhat poset, hence nilpotent; the $(x,w)$ entry of $N^m$ is the sum of products over chains of $m$ strict steps. Therefore $$Q'=I-N+N^2-\cdots+(-1)^M N^M=(I+N)^{-1}=P^{-1},$$ where $M$ can be any integer at least the maximum strict-chain length. In particular, $Q'P=PQ'=I$ and $$\sum_zq'_{x,z}p_{z,w}=\delta_{x,w}=\sum_zp_{x,z}q'_{z,w}.$$

The **inverse Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials** in the classical sign convention are $q_{x,w}:=\mathrm{sgn}(x)\mathrm{sgn}(w)q'_{x,w}$. If $\Sigma$ is the diagonal matrix with entries $\Sigma_{x,x}=\mathrm{sgn}(x)$, then $Q=(q_{x,w})=\Sigma Q'\Sigma$. Equivalently, if $D_x$ is the basis of $H^*=\mathrm{Hom}_A(H,A)$ dual to the Kazhdan–Lusztig basis, then $$q'_{x,w}=D_x(H_w),$$ since $H_w=\sum_zq'_{z,w}\underline H_z$.

Let $P=(p_{x,w})$, $Q'=(q'_{x,w})$ and $R=(r_{x,y})$ be the triangular matrices of [[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-the-kazhdan-lusztig-basis]], [[def-inverse-kazhdan-lusztig-polynomials]] and [[thm-r-polynomial-recursion-and-degree-bounds]]. Then (a) $P=R\bar P$, $\bar P=\bar RP$, and $R\bar R=\bar RR=1$; (b) $Q'P=PQ'=1$, and the inversion formulas $$\overline{q'_{x,w}}=\sum_{x\le z\le w}q'_{x,z}r_{z,w},\qquad \overline{q_{x,w}}=\sum_{x\le z\le w}q_{x,z}\overline{r_{z,w}}$$ hold, i.e. $\bar Q'=Q'R$ and $\bar Q=Q\bar R$; (c) for the dual basis $D_x(\underline H_w)=\delta_{x,w}$ from [[def-inverse-kazhdan-lusztig-polynomials]], $D_x(H_w)=q'_{x,w}$. The inversion is proved from the bar-duality relations alone (no finite case check).

Identify $\mathbb Z[q]$ with $\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$ by $q\mapsto v^{-2}$. For $y\le w$ in $S_n$, put $d=\ell(w)-\ell(y)$ and define the **Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomial** $P_{y,w}(q)\in\mathbb Z[q]$ by $$P_{y,w}(v^{-2})=v^{-d}p_{y,w},$$ where $\underline H_w=\sum_{y\le w}p_{y,w}H_y$ is the Kazhdan–Lusztig basis of [[lem-type-a-kazhdan-lusztig-basis-has-elementary-triangular-bar-properties]]. The parity clause of that theorem makes the right side a polynomial in $v^{-2}$. The conventions are: $P_{y,w}=0$ unless $y\le w$, $P_{w,w}=1$, $P_{y,w}$ has constant term 1, and for $y<w$ its degree is at most $(\ell(w)-\ell(y)-1)/2$. The **$\mu$-coefficient** is $$\mu(y,w):=	ext{coefficient of }q^{(\ell(w)-\ell(y)-1)/2}	ext{ in }P_{y,w},$$ defined to be 0 when $\ell(w)-\ell(y)$ is even; equivalently $\mu(y,w)$ is the coefficient of $v$ in $p_{y,w}$. One writes $\mu(y|w)
e0$ when $y
e w$ and ($y<w$ and $\mu(y,w)
e0$) or ($w<y$ and $\mu(w,y)
e0$). The dictionary with the literature is recorded for use: with the classical parameter $T_s^2=(q-1)T_s+q$ one has $H_w=v^{\ell(w)}T_w$, the element $\underline H_w$ is the basis element $C'_w$ of [EW], and $h_{y,w}=p_{y,w}$ with $v^{\ell(w)-\ell(y)}P_{y,w}(v^{-2})=h_{y,w}$ [EW, Remark 3.2].

Let $\le$ be the rank-inequality order on the zero-based $S_n$ of [[def-bruhat-order-on-the-symmetric-group]], and identify it with the one-based realization by shifting inputs and values by $1$. (a) This order is the strong Bruhat order of type A: the transitive closure of covers $x\to tx$ where $t$ is a transposition and $\ell(tx)=\ell(x)+1$. (b) If $y\le w$ then $\ell(y)\le\ell(w)$, with equality iff $y=w$; every saturated chain has $\ell(w)-\ell(y)$ steps; and $y\le w$ iff $y^{-1}\le w^{-1}$. (c) $y\le w$ iff for every reduced expression $w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k}$, $y$ is a reduced subword. (d) For every simple reflection $s$, if $y\le w$ and $\ell(sy)>\ell(y)$, then $y\le sw$; if $y\le w$ and $\ell(sw)<\ell(w)$, then $sy\le w$. (e) Every interval $[y,w]$ is finite; if $y\le w$, then $[y,w]=\{y\}\cup\bigcup_{y\to a\le w}[a,w]$.

Let $s=s_i$ be a simple reflection, $w\in S_n$ with $sw<w$, and $y\le w$. With $P_{x,z}:=0$ whenever $x\not\le z$, $$P_{y,w}(q)=q^{1-c}P_{sy,sw}(q)+q^{c}P_{y,sw}(q)-\!\!\!\sum_{\substack{y\le z\le sw\\ sz<z,\ \mu(z,sw)\ne0}}\!\!\!\mu(z,sw)\,q^{(\ell(w)-\ell(z))/2}P_{y,z}(q),$$ where $c=1$ if $sy<y$ and $c=0$ if $sy>y$; here $\mu$ is the coefficient defined in [[def-kazhdan-lusztig-polynomials-in-the-classical-q-normalization]] (so the summand only occurs for $\ell(sw)-\ell(z)$ odd, and $(\ell(w)-\ell(z))/2$ is then an integer). The same recursion holds with $s\in R(w)$ (right descents) after replacing each index $x$ by $x^{-1}$, using $P_{y^{-1},w^{-1}}=P_{y,w}$ and $\mu(y^{-1},w^{-1})=\mu(y,w)$.

Fix a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ of type
$A_{n-1}$ with Cartan $\mathfrak h$, positive system $\Phi^+$, Weyl vector
$\rho$, Weyl group $W$ (identified with $S_n$) and dot action
$w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$. Fix a dominant regular integral weight
$\lambda$, i.e. $\langle\lambda+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle\neq0$ for every root and
$\lambda$ integral, and let $\mathcal O_\lambda$ be the corresponding regular
integral block in the conventions of
[[def-regular-integral-category-o-block-and-its-antidominant-weight]]: standard
objects $\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)=M(w\cdot\lambda)$, simples $L(w\cdot\lambda)$,
indecomposable projectives $P(w\cdot\lambda)$ for $w\in W$, with
$\lambda=e\cdot\lambda$ the unique dominant and $w_0\cdot\lambda$ the unique
antidominant element and $\Delta(w_0\cdot\lambda)=L(w_0\cdot\lambda)$.

This item freezes the following conventions, each inherited from the cited
suppliers and used verbatim below.

(i) **Multiplicity conventions.** $(P(w\cdot\lambda):\Delta(y\cdot\lambda))$ is
the Verma-flag multiplicity of [[def-verma-flag-and-its-multiplicities]] and
$[M(y\cdot\lambda):L(w\cdot\lambda)]$ the composition multiplicity, and
$$(P(w\cdot\lambda):\Delta(y\cdot\lambda))=[M(y\cdot\lambda):L(w\cdot\lambda)]$$
by BGG reciprocity ([[thm-bgg-reciprocity]]).

(ii) **Bruhat reversal convention.** Along the bijection
$W\ni w\mapsto w\cdot\lambda$ the Bruhat order runs opposite to the dominance
order, in the two exact senses used on this page: $y\le w$ implies

the finiteness of intervals of the Bruhat order

([[def-kazhdan-lusztig-polynomials-in-the-classical-q-normalization]]), support

symmetry $p_{y^{-1},w^{-1}}=p_{y,w}$.

polynomial standard graph bimodule supported at $x$, and $B_x$ for the
normalized indecomposable polynomial Soergel bimodule, which is generally not a
standard graph bimodule. With right reduction $\bar B=B\otimes_S\mathbb C$
and left coinvariant-module values of $V$, the projective dictionary is
$$V(P(w\cdot\lambda))\cong\bar B_{w^{-1}}$$
([[thm-indecomposable-projectives-correspond-to-indecomposable-soergel-modules]]).
The graph label $x$ corresponds to the standard
$\Delta(x^{-1}\cdot\lambda)$. The individual support ranks are measured on the
polynomial lift before reduction, as in
[[prop-verma-flag-multiplicities-are-standard-filtration-ranks-under-v]];
no separated graph-support filtration of the reduced module is asserted.

For degree bookkeeping use precisely the standard-generator normalization of
[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]]:
$\Delta_x(d)=R_x(d-\ell(x))$, and $r_{x,d}(B)$ counts these normalized polynomial
standard layers. Thus the coefficient polynomial is
$$m_x(B;v):=\sum_d r_{x,d}(B)v^d,\qquad h_\Delta(B)=\sum_xm_x(B;v)\widetilde T_x,\qquad\widetilde T_x=v^{\ell(x)}T_x.$$
Here $\widetilde T_x$ is the normalized **standard** Hecke element $H_x$ used
in clause (iii) and
[[def-normalized-type-a-hecke-algebra-and-its-bar-involution]]. The published
Soergel split-Grothendieck-ring convention instead names its simple
Kazhdan--Lusztig generators $H_i=v(T_i+1)=\widetilde T_{s_i}+v$; these must not
be confused with the standard element $H_{s_i}=vT_i$
([[thm-split-grothendieck-group-of-the-soergel-category-is-the-type-a-hecke-algebra]]).

used to identify $h_\Delta(B_x)$ with $\underline H_x$; a product of simple
Soergel classes is a Bott--Samelson class and need not be $[B_x]$.

gradings only; forgetting them gives the ordinary projective dictionary.

derivations.claim: By [F1] the class of every standard in $K_0(\mathcal O_\lambda)$ expands in the simple basis as $[M(y\cdot\lambda)]=\sum_w[M(y\cdot\lambda):L(w\cdot\lambda)]\,[L(w\cdot\lambda)]=\sum_wA_{y,w}[L(w\cdot\lambda)]$, where $A_{y,w}=P_{y,w}(1)$; by [F4] and [F7] the matrix $A$ is unitriangular for the Bruhat order: $A_{w,w}=1$ and $A_{y,w}=0$ unless $y\le w$.

The matrix $A$ is the specialization at $v=1$ of the Kazhdan–Lusztig coefficient matrix $P=(p_{x,w})$, because $p_{y,w}(1)=P_{y,w}(1)$ by [F4]; specialisation $v\mapsto1$ is a ring homomorphism $\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to\mathbb Z$, so the inverse matrix of $A$ is $A^{-1}=Q'(1)=(q'_{x,w}(1))$ by the two-sided inverse statement $Q'=P^{-1}$ of [F3]. By the support clause of [F3], $q'_{w,x}(1)=0$ unless $w\le x$, and all entries are integers; in particular the sum in the formula is supported on $x\ge w$, and every coefficient $q'_{w,x}(1)$ is the value at one of an integer Laurent polynomial.

The specialization is not the Möbius function in general; the following finite witness is computed inside $S_4$ with the recursion [F6]. Put $b:=1324=s_2$ and $T:=3412=s_2s_1s_3s_2$; the reduced subwords of this reduced word for $T$ give the interval $[b,T]=\{1324;\ 1342,1423,2314,3124;\ 1432,2413,3142,3214;\ 3412\}$, ten elements, and all comparable pairs of gap at most two have $P=1$ by the degree bound of [F4], so the only pair that can be nonconstant is the endpoint $(b,T)$, of gap $3$. Apply [F6] with the left descent $s=s_2$ of $T$: $s_2T=2413$, $s_2b=1234$ and $c=1$, so $P_{b,T}=P_{1234,2413}+qP_{b,2413}-\sum_z\mu(z,2413)q^{(4-\ell(z))/2}P_{b,z}$, where $z$ runs over the elements of $[b,2413]=\{1324,1423,2314,2413\}$ with $s_2z<z$; left multiplication by $s_2$ swaps the values $2$ and $3$, turning these four elements into $1234,1432,3214,3412$ of lengths $0,3,3,4$, so only $z=b$ has the required descent, and there $\mu(b,2413)=0$ because the gap $2$ is even by [F4]. Hence the correction sum vanishes, and with $P_{b,2413}=1$ (gap $2$) the recursion reduces to $P_{b,T}=P_{1234,2413}+q$. For the remaining value apply [F6] at $(1234,2413)$ with the left descent $s_1$: $s_12413=1423$ and $c=0$, so $P_{1234,2413}=qP_{2134,1423}+P_{1234,1423}-\sum_{z}\mu(z,1423)q^{(3-\ell(z))/2}P_{1234,z}$; the first term vanishes because $1423=s_3s_2$ has no reduced subword $s_1$, so $2134\not\le1423$ and $P_{2134,1423}=0$ by [F4] and [F5], and the correction sum is empty because the four elements of $[1234,1423]=\{1234,1324,1243,1423\}$ all have lengths $0,1,1,2$ raised to $1,2,2,3$ by left multiplication with $s_1$, so none is a left descent. Thus $P_{1234,2413}=1$, and altogether $P_{b,T}(q)=1+q$, while $P_{y,z}=1$ for every other comparable pair in $[b,T]$.

Since the classes $[L(w\cdot\lambda)]$ and $[M(x\cdot\lambda)]$ are the two $\mathbb Z$-bases of the Grothendieck group of the block by [F2], step 1.1 exhibits the transition matrix from simples to standards, and its inverse from step 1.2 performs the reverse change of basis: for every $w\in W$ one has $[L(w\cdot\lambda)]=\sum_xq'_{w,x}(1)\,[M(x\cdot\lambda)]$, the sum being finite and supported on $x\ge w$ by [F5] and step 1.2. Applying the additive character map of [F2] termwise gives the equivalent formal-character identity $\mathrm{ch}\,L(w\cdot\lambda)=\sum_xq'_{w,x}(1)\,\mathrm{ch}\,M(x\cdot\lambda)$. In the signed normalization $q_{x,w}=\mathrm{sgn}(x)\mathrm{sgn}(w)q'_{x,w}$ of [F3], substituting $q'_{w,x}(1)=(-1)^{\ell(w)+\ell(x)}q_{w,x}(1)$ and using that $\ell(w)+\ell(x)$ and $\ell(w)-\ell(x)$ differ by the even number $2\ell(x)$ gives the signed inverse-Kazhdan–Lusztig sum $\mathrm{ch}\,L(w\cdot\lambda)=\sum_{x\ge w}(-1)^{\ell(w)-\ell(x)}q_{w,x}(1)\,\mathrm{ch}\,M(x\cdot\lambda)$.

The chain formula of [F3] expresses the inverse coefficients of step 2.1 as the weighted incidence-algebra inverse of $A$: $q'_{x,w}(1)=\sum_{m\ge0}(-1)^m\sum_{x=z_0<z_1<\cdots<z_m=w}P_{z_0,z_1}(1)\cdots P_{z_{m-1},z_m}(1)$, a finite sum over the strictly increasing chains of the finite interval $[x,w]$ described in [F5]. If every comparable-pair value $P_{y,z}(1)$ in $[x,w]$ equals $1$, each product in the $m$-th term equals $1$ and the alternating chain count $\sum_m(-1)^m\#\{\text{strictly increasing chains }x=z_0<\cdots<z_m=w\}$ is exactly the ordinary Bruhat Möbius value $\mu(x,w)$; so on intervals with all comparable-pair values equal to $1$ the coefficients are ordinary Bruhat Möbius numbers.

Consequently the specialized multiplicity matrix on the interval $[b,T]$ is $A=Z+E$, where $Z$ is the zeta matrix of the Bruhat poset and $E$ has the single nonzero entry $1$ at $(b,T)$. Since $b$ is the minimum and $T$ the maximum of the interval, $Z_{x,b}=1$ only for $x=b$ and $Z_{T,x}=1$ only for $x=T$, so $EZ^{-1}=E=ZE$ and $(Z+E)(Z^{-1}-E)=I-ZE+EZ^{-1}=I$, that is $A^{-1}=Z^{-1}-E$; at the endpoint the inverse entry is therefore $\mu(b,T)-1=-1-1=-2$, whereas the ordinary Bruhat Möbius value of the interval is $\mu(b,T)=-1$ (the rank sizes are $1,4,4,1$ and the Möbius recursion gives $1$ at the bottom, $-1$ at the four atoms, $+1$ at the four rank-two elements and $-(1-4+4)=-1$ at the top). Using the endpoint polynomial from step 1.3, this proves the claim that the coefficients specialize to ordinary Bruhat Möbius values when all comparable-pair values are $1$ but not in general, and exhibits them as integers that may be negative; by step 2.1 these are exactly the coefficients of the character formula, and only their value at $q=1$ occurs.

For $n=1$, set $H_v(1):=A$.

Here $S_n=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\ldots,n\})$, $s_i=(i\ i+1)$, and $\ell$ is inversion length as in [[def-symmetric-group]] and [[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]. For $w\in S_n$, let $T_w$ be the standard basis element of the generic Hecke algebra of [[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]], formed from any reduced expression of $w$, and after the coefficient specialization $q\mapsto v^{-2}$ put $H_w:=v^{\ell(w)}T_w$. Equivalently, $H_w=H_{s_{i_1}}\cdots H_{s_{i_k}}$ for a reduced expression $w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k}$. The standard-basis theorem [[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]] and rescaling by units show that $\{H_w:w\in S_n\}$ is an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$.

Right multiplication by a generator is
$$H_wH_{s_i}=H_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)+1,\qquad H_wH_{s_i}=H_{ws_i}+(v^{-1}-v)H_w\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)-1.$$

[[thm-projectives-in-category-o-have-verma-flags]], and the right-hand
multiplicity is the simple composition multiplicity of the Verma module
$M(\mu)$ ([[def-standard-and-costandard-objects-in-category-o]]).

For $\lambda\in\mathfrak h^*$, the **Verma module** is the induced
$\mathfrak g$-module

$$M(\lambda):=U(\mathfrak g)\otimes_{U(\mathfrak b)}\mathbb C_\lambda,$$

where $U(\mathfrak g)$ is the quotient algebra of
[[def-universal-enveloping-algebra-as-a-tensor-quotient]] and
$\mathbb C_\lambda$ is [[def-one-dimensional-borel-module-of-weight-lambda]].
Write $v_\lambda:=1\otimes c_\lambda$.  Thus $M(\lambda)$ is the quotient of
$U(\mathfrak g)$ by the left ideal generated by $x$ for $x\in\mathfrak n^+$
and $h-\lambda(h)$ for $h\in\mathfrak h$; in particular,
$\mathfrak n^+v_\lambda=0$ and $hv_\lambda=\lambda(h)v_\lambda$.

Fix a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ of type
$A_{n-1}$ with Cartan $\mathfrak h$, positive system $\Phi^+$, Weyl vector
$\rho$, Weyl group $W$ (identified with $S_n$) and dot action
$w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$. Fix a dominant regular integral weight
$\lambda$, i.e. $\langle\lambda+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle\neq0$ for every root and
$\lambda$ integral, and let $\mathcal O_\lambda$ be the corresponding regular
integral block in the conventions of
[[def-regular-integral-category-o-block-and-its-antidominant-weight]]: standard
objects $\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)=M(w\cdot\lambda)$, simples $L(w\cdot\lambda)$,
indecomposable projectives $P(w\cdot\lambda)$ for $w\in W$, with
$\lambda=e\cdot\lambda$ the unique dominant and $w_0\cdot\lambda$ the unique
antidominant element and $\Delta(w_0\cdot\lambda)=L(w_0\cdot\lambda)$.

This item freezes the following conventions, each inherited from the cited
suppliers and used verbatim below.

(i) **Multiplicity conventions.** $(P(w\cdot\lambda):\Delta(y\cdot\lambda))$ is
the Verma-flag multiplicity of [[def-verma-flag-and-its-multiplicities]] and
$[M(y\cdot\lambda):L(w\cdot\lambda)]$ the composition multiplicity, and
$$(P(w\cdot\lambda):\Delta(y\cdot\lambda))=[M(y\cdot\lambda):L(w\cdot\lambda)]$$
by BGG reciprocity ([[thm-bgg-reciprocity]]).

(ii) **Bruhat reversal convention.** Along the bijection
$W\ni w\mapsto w\cdot\lambda$ the Bruhat order runs opposite to the dominance
order, in the two exact senses used on this page: $y\le w$ implies
$w\cdot\lambda\le y\cdot\lambda$ in the dominance order, and every nonzero
multiplicity forces the index direction, i.e.
$[M(y\cdot\lambda):L(w\cdot\lambda)]\neq0$ implies $y\le w$ in the Bruhat
order. The first sense is the inclusion direction of
[[lem-dominant-integral-dot-translates-embed-in-the-verma-module]] (for
$w\ge y$ one has $M(w\cdot\lambda)\subseteq M(y\cdot\lambda)$, so the highest
weight of the submodule is the lower one), and the second is
[[lem-jordan-holder-factors-of-verma-modules-lie-above-the-head]], which
confines every composition factor of $M(y\cdot\lambda)$ to labels
$w\ge y$. The full statement that the two orders are isomorphic as posets is
not needed here and is not asserted; only these two directions, together with
the finiteness of intervals of the Bruhat order
([[lem-bruhat-order-basic-properties-for-permutations]]), are used.

(iii) **Hecke and Kazhdan–Lusztig normalization.** The Kazhdan–Lusztig basis
$\underline H_w=\sum_{y\le w}p_{y,w}H_y$ of the normalized type-$A$ Hecke
algebra ([[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-the-kazhdan-lusztig-basis]]), with
$$p_{y,w}=v^{\ell(w)-\ell(y)}P_{y,w}(v^{-2})$$
in the classical $q=v^{-2}$ normalization
([[def-kazhdan-lusztig-polynomials-in-the-classical-q-normalization]]), support
$p_{y,w}=0$ unless $y\le w$, diagonal $p_{w,w}=1$, and simultaneous inversion
symmetry $p_{y^{-1},w^{-1}}=p_{y,w}$.

(iv) **Soergel label and character dictionary.** Write $R_x$ for the
polynomial standard graph bimodule supported at $x$, and $B_x$ for the
normalized indecomposable polynomial Soergel bimodule, which is generally not a
standard graph bimodule. With right reduction $\bar B=B\otimes_S\mathbb C$
and left coinvariant-module values of $V$, the projective dictionary is
$$V(P(w\cdot\lambda))\cong\bar B_{w^{-1}}$$
([[thm-indecomposable-projectives-correspond-to-indecomposable-soergel-modules]]).
The graph label $x$ corresponds to the standard
$\Delta(x^{-1}\cdot\lambda)$. The individual support ranks are measured on the
polynomial lift before reduction, as in
[[prop-verma-flag-multiplicities-are-standard-filtration-ranks-under-v]];
no separated graph-support filtration of the reduced module is asserted.

For degree bookkeeping use precisely the standard-generator normalization of
[[def-type-a-standard-graph-bimodules-support-filtrations-and-character]]:
$\Delta_x(d)=R_x(d-\ell(x))$, and $r_{x,d}(B)$ counts these normalized polynomial
standard layers. Thus the coefficient polynomial is
$$m_x(B;v):=\sum_d r_{x,d}(B)v^d,\qquad h_\Delta(B)=\sum_xm_x(B;v)\widetilde T_x,\qquad\widetilde T_x=v^{\ell(x)}T_x.$$
Here $\widetilde T_x$ is the normalized **standard** Hecke element $H_x$ used
in clause (iii) and
[[def-normalized-type-a-hecke-algebra-and-its-bar-involution]]. The published
Soergel split-Grothendieck-ring convention instead names its simple
Kazhdan--Lusztig generators $H_i=v(T_i+1)=\widetilde T_{s_i}+v$; these must not
be confused with the standard element $H_{s_i}=vT_i$
([[thm-split-grothendieck-group-of-the-soergel-category-is-the-type-a-hecke-algebra]]).
The standard-character supplier
[[lem-the-type-a-standard-character-is-multiplicative]] identifies $h_\Delta$
with that split-Grothendieck-ring isomorphism. This records the coefficient
normalization, and does not infer the image of a general indecomposable $B_x$
by multiplying simple generators. In particular the character theorem must be
used to identify $h_\Delta(B_x)$ with $\underline H_x$; a product of simple
Soergel classes is a Bott--Samelson class and need not be $[B_x]$.
The inverse labels and all rank comparisons above use auxiliary polynomial
gradings only; forgetting them gives the ordinary projective dictionary.

derivations.claim: **The dot orbit.** With $\rho=\alpha_1+\alpha_2$ for the root system $A_2$, the dot action $w\cdot0=w(\rho)-\rho$ computes: $123\cdot0=0$; $213\cdot0=s_1(\rho)-\rho=-\alpha_1$; $132\cdot0=s_2(\rho)-\rho=-\alpha_2$; $231\cdot0=(s_1s_2)\cdot0=s_1\cdot(-\alpha_2)=s_1(\rho-\alpha_2)-\rho=-2\alpha_1-\alpha_2$; $312\cdot0=(s_2s_1)\cdot0=-\alpha_1-2\alpha_2$; $321\cdot0=w_0(\rho)-\rho=-2\rho$. The positive-root pairings of $\rho$ are $1,1,2$, and the negative-root pairings are their negatives; Weyl conjugation permutes these nonzero integral pairings, so all six weights are dot-regular and integral, so $\mathcal O_0$ is a regular integral block with the six labelled standards, simples and projectives.

**The Kazhdan–Lusztig basis of $H_v(3)$.** Put $X=H_{213}$, $Y=H_{132}$ and $A:=X+v$, $B:=Y+v$; by [F1] both $A$ and $B$ are bar-fixed, because $\overline{X+v}=(X+\alpha)+v^{-1}=X+v$ and likewise for $Y$. The reduced words give $H_{231}=XY$, $H_{312}=YX$ and $H_{321}=YXY$ in the one-based model, so $AB=H_{231}+v(H_{213}+H_{132})+v^2H_{123}$ and $BA=H_{312}+v(H_{132}+H_{213})+v^2H_{123}$. For the length-three element, expanding $(Y+v)(X+v)(Y+v)$ and replacing $Y^2$ by $1-\alpha Y$ gives $BAB=H_{321}+v(H_{231}+H_{312})+(1+v^2)H_{132}+v^2H_{213}+(v+v^3)H_{123}$, hence $BAB-B=H_{321}+v(H_{231}+H_{312})+v^2(H_{132}+H_{213})+v^3H_{123}$. Each of the six elements $H_{123}$, $A$, $B$, $AB$, $BA$, $BAB-B$ is bar-fixed and lies in its top standard basis element plus a $v\mathbb Z[v]$-span of strictly lower Bruhat elements (the lower indices are strictly lower by the rank description of [F4]); by the uniqueness in [F2] they are exactly $\underline H_{123},\underline H_{213},\underline H_{132},\underline H_{231},\underline H_{312},\underline H_{321}$.

**All polynomials equal $1$, and the count.** Reading the six expansions of step 1.2 against $\underline H_w=\sum_{y\le w}p_{y,w}H_y$ gives $p_{y,w}=v^{\ell(w)-\ell(y)}$ whenever $y\le w$: the coefficients are $1$ on the diagonal, $v$ at gap one, $v^2$ at gap two and $v^3$ at the longest pair. Hence [F3] gives $P_{y,w}(q)=1$ for every one of the comparable pairs. By the rank description [F4] the comparable pairs are: the six diagonal pairs; for $y=123$ the five strict pairs; for each of $y=213,132$ the three strict pairs (the two rank-two elements and $321$); and for each of $y=231,312$ the pair with $321$; altogether $6+5+3+3+1+1=19$ pairs, and every one has $P_{y,w}=1$.

**The multiplicity matrix.** By [F5] and step 2.1, $[M(y\cdot0):L(w\cdot0)]=P_{y,w}(1)=1$ exactly when $y\le w$ and $0$ otherwise; this is the Bruhat zeta matrix of $S_3$ with rows $y$ and columns $w$. For the displayed instances: $y=123$ is the minimum of the Bruhat order, so $[M(0):L(w\cdot0)]=1$ for all six $w$; $y=321$ is the maximum, so $[M(321\cdot0):L(w\cdot0)]=0$ unless $w=321$, where it is $1$; and for $y=213$ the comparable columns are $w=213,231,312,321$ by [F4], so $M(213\cdot0)$ has exactly the four composition factors $L(213\cdot0),L(231\cdot0),L(312\cdot0),L(321\cdot0)$, each once.

**The Verma-flag matrix.** Applying BGG reciprocity [F6] with $\mu=w\cdot0$ and $\nu=y\cdot0$ gives $(P(w\cdot0):\Delta(y\cdot0))=[M(y\cdot0):L(w\cdot0)]$, which by step 3.1 is $1$ exactly when $y\le w$ and $0$ otherwise; the interpretation of the left-hand multiplicity is the Verma-flag multiplicity of the labelled projective by [F7]. In particular $(P(123\cdot0):\Delta(y\cdot0))=0$ for $y\ne123$ (with value $1$ at $y=123$, since $123$ is the minimum and no other $y$ lies below it) and $(P(321\cdot0):\Delta(y\cdot0))=1$ for all $y$ (all $y$ lie below the maximum $321$). So the projective-flag matrix is the same zeta matrix.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. In a regular integral type-$A$ block
$\mathcal O_\lambda$, for every $w\in W$ the class of $L(w\cdot\lambda)$ in the
Grothendieck group, equivalently its formal character, is
$$[L(w\cdot\lambda)]=\sum_{x\in W}q'_{w,x}(1)\,[M(x\cdot\lambda)],\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \mathrm{ch}\,L(w\cdot\lambda)=\sum_{x\in W}q'_{w,x}(1)\,\mathrm{ch}\,M(x\cdot\lambda),$$
where $q'_{x,w}$ are the inverse Kazhdan–Lusztig coefficients of
[[def-inverse-kazhdan-lusztig-polynomials]] ($Q'=P^{-1}$, $q'_{x,w}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$
for $x<w$, $q'_{w,w}=1$) and the sum is supported on $x\ge w$. Equivalently, in
the signed normalization $q_{x,w}=\mathrm{sgn}(x)\mathrm{sgn}(w)q'_{x,w}$ the
formula is the signed inverse-Kazhdan–Lusztig sum
$$\mathrm{ch}\,L(w\cdot\lambda)=\sum_{x\ge w}(-1)^{\ell(w)-\ell(x)}q_{w,x}(1)\,\mathrm{ch}\,M(x\cdot\lambda).$$
The coefficients $q'_{w,x}(1)$ are the weighted incidence-algebra inverse of
$(P_{y,z}(1))$, given by the finite signed chain sum of products of
$P_{y,z}(1)$; they are integers that may be negative. They specialize to
ordinary Bruhat Möbius values on intervals where every comparable-pair
Kazhdan–Lusztig value is $1$, but not in general. Only the value at $q=1$
occurs.

Take $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{sl}_3$ (type $A_2$, $W=S_3$) and the principal block,
i.e. the regular integral block $\mathcal O_0$ of the weight $\lambda=0$
($0+\rho=\rho$ is regular). In one-line notation the labels
$w\in\{123,213,132,231,312,321\}$ index the weights
$w\cdot0=0,-\alpha_1,-\alpha_2,-2\alpha_1-\alpha_2,-\alpha_1-2\alpha_2,-2\rho$.
All nineteen Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials of comparable pairs in $S_3$ equal
$1$ (there are nineteen pairs $y\le w$ in the Bruhat order on $S_3$), so
$$[M(y\cdot0):L(w\cdot0)]=P_{y,w}(1)=1\ \text{ if } y\le w,\qquad 0\ \text{ otherwise}:$$
the multiplicity matrix is the Bruhat zeta matrix of $S_3$ (with rows $y$,
columns $w$), e.g. $[M(0):L(w\cdot0)]=1$ for all six $w$,
$[M(321\cdot0):L(w\cdot0)]=0$ unless $w=321$, and $M(213\cdot0)$ has the four
composition factors $L(213\cdot0),L(231\cdot0),L(312\cdot0),L(321\cdot0)$, each
once. By BGG reciprocity the Verma-flag matrix
$(P(w\cdot0):\Delta(y\cdot0))$ is the same zeta matrix, e.g.
$(P(123\cdot0):\Delta(y\cdot0))=0$ for $y\ne123$ and
$(P(321\cdot0):\Delta(y\cdot0))=1$ for all $y$.

For $x,w\in S_n$ set $$q'_{x,w}:=\sum_{m\ge0}(-1)^m\sum_{x=z_0<z_1<\cdots<z_m=w}p_{z_0,z_1}p_{z_1,z_2}\cdots p_{z_{m-1},z_m}\in A,$$ where the inner sum is over strictly increasing Bruhat chains from $x$ to $w$, the $m=0$ chain occurs only when $x=w$, and $p_{u,v}$ are the coefficients of the Kazhdan–Lusztig basis ([[lem-type-a-kazhdan-lusztig-basis-has-elementary-triangular-bar-properties]]). Every chain lies in a finite Bruhat interval by [[lem-bruhat-order-basic-properties-for-permutations]], so the sum is finite. If $x\not\le w$ there are no chains; if $x=w$, the empty chain gives $q'_{w,w}=1$. If $x<w$, each chain has at least one factor $p_{u,v}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ with $u<v$, so $q'_{x,w}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$.

Let $P=(p_{x,w})$ and $Q'=(q'_{x,w})$. The matrix $N:=P-I$ is strictly triangular on the finite Bruhat poset, hence nilpotent; the $(x,w)$ entry of $N^m$ is the sum of products over chains of $m$ strict steps. Therefore $$Q'=I-N+N^2-\cdots+(-1)^M N^M=(I+N)^{-1}=P^{-1},$$ where $M$ can be any integer at least the maximum strict-chain length. In particular, $Q'P=PQ'=I$ and $$\sum_zq'_{x,z}p_{z,w}=\delta_{x,w}=\sum_zp_{x,z}q'_{z,w}.$$

The **inverse Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials** in the classical sign convention are $q_{x,w}:=\mathrm{sgn}(x)\mathrm{sgn}(w)q'_{x,w}$. If $\Sigma$ is the diagonal matrix with entries $\Sigma_{x,x}=\mathrm{sgn}(x)$, then $Q=(q_{x,w})=\Sigma Q'\Sigma$. Equivalently, if $D_x$ is the basis of $H^*=\mathrm{Hom}_A(H,A)$ dual to the Kazhdan–Lusztig basis, then $$q'_{x,w}=D_x(H_w),$$ since $H_w=\sum_zq'_{z,w}\underline H_z$.

Let $P=(p_{x,w})$, $Q'=(q'_{x,w})$ and $R=(r_{x,y})$ be the triangular matrices of [[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-the-kazhdan-lusztig-basis]], [[def-inverse-kazhdan-lusztig-polynomials]] and [[thm-r-polynomial-recursion-and-degree-bounds]]. Then (a) $P=R\bar P$, $\bar P=\bar RP$, and $R\bar R=\bar RR=1$; (b) $Q'P=PQ'=1$, and the inversion formulas $$\overline{q'_{x,w}}=\sum_{x\le z\le w}q'_{x,z}r_{z,w},\qquad \overline{q_{x,w}}=\sum_{x\le z\le w}q_{x,z}\overline{r_{z,w}}$$ hold, i.e. $\bar Q'=Q'R$ and $\bar Q=Q\bar R$; (c) for the dual basis $D_x(\underline H_w)=\delta_{x,w}$ from [[def-inverse-kazhdan-lusztig-polynomials]], $D_x(H_w)=q'_{x,w}$. The inversion is proved from the bar-duality relations alone (no finite case check).

Identify $\mathbb Z[q]$ with $\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$ by $q\mapsto v^{-2}$. For $y\le w$ in $S_n$, put $d=\ell(w)-\ell(y)$ and define the **Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomial** $P_{y,w}(q)\in\mathbb Z[q]$ by $$P_{y,w}(v^{-2})=v^{-d}p_{y,w},$$ where $\underline H_w=\sum_{y\le w}p_{y,w}H_y$ is the Kazhdan–Lusztig basis of [[lem-type-a-kazhdan-lusztig-basis-has-elementary-triangular-bar-properties]]. The parity clause of that theorem makes the right side a polynomial in $v^{-2}$. The conventions are: $P_{y,w}=0$ unless $y\le w$, $P_{w,w}=1$, $P_{y,w}$ has constant term 1, and for $y<w$ its degree is at most $(\ell(w)-\ell(y)-1)/2$. The **$\mu$-coefficient** is $$\mu(y,w):=	ext{coefficient of }q^{(\ell(w)-\ell(y)-1)/2}	ext{ in }P_{y,w},$$ defined to be 0 when $\ell(w)-\ell(y)$ is even; equivalently $\mu(y,w)$ is the coefficient of $v$ in $p_{y,w}$. One writes $\mu(y|w)
e0$ when $y
e w$ and ($y<w$ and $\mu(y,w)
e0$) or ($w<y$ and $\mu(w,y)
e0$). The dictionary with the literature is recorded for use: with the classical parameter $T_s^2=(q-1)T_s+q$ one has $H_w=v^{\ell(w)}T_w$, the element $\underline H_w$ is the basis element $C'_w$ of [EW], and $h_{y,w}=p_{y,w}$ with $v^{\ell(w)-\ell(y)}P_{y,w}(v^{-2})=h_{y,w}$ [EW, Remark 3.2].

Fix a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, and a positive Borel $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$. Write $Q^+=\sum_i\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\alpha_i$, $\mu\leq\lambda$ when $\lambda-\mu\in Q^+$, and $w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$.

For the abelian category [[thm-category-o-is-abelian-and-extension-closed]], define $K_0(\mathcal O)$ as the free abelian group on isomorphism classes $[M]$, modulo $[B]=[A]+[C]$ for every short exact sequence $0\to A\to B\to C\to0$. A set of representatives suffices: every finitely generated $U(\mathfrak g)$-module is a quotient of some $U(\mathfrak g)^n$, and those quotients form a set up to isomorphism.

Define the formal character by $\operatorname{ch}M=\sum_\mu(\dim M_\mu)e^\mu$. By [[prop-equivalent-support-description-of-category-o]], its integer coefficients are finite and supported in finitely many downward cones. Let $\mathscr R$ be the group of all such integer coefficient families, with pointwise addition. It is a ring with $e^\mu e^\nu=e^{\mu+\nu}$: at a fixed resulting weight, in any pair of cones the equation $\beta+\gamma=\eta$ with $\beta,\gamma\in Q^+$ has finitely many solutions, since every simple-root coefficient is bounded. Taking weight spaces is exact, so character gives a well-defined homomorphism $K_0(\mathcal O)\to\mathscr R$. The zero object's class and character are zero.

Assume the Axiom of Choice.

Fix a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, and a positive Borel $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$. Write $Q^+=\sum_i\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\alpha_i$, $\mu\leq\lambda$ when $\lambda-\mu\in Q^+$, and $w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$.

The classes $[L(\lambda)]$, and separately the classes $[M(\lambda)]$, form $\mathbb Z$-bases of $K_0(\mathcal O)$. For a fixed finite central-character label set $\Lambda=W\cdot\lambda$, the transition between its standard and simple classes is unitriangular in any linear order extending $\leq$. This remains true on a downward-closed subset of that finite poset. It is not a claim about finite downward ideals of all of $\mathfrak h^*$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\lambda\in\Lambda^+$. In the Grothendieck group of the linkage block of $\lambda$ ([[def-grothendieck-group-and-character-of-category-o]], [[prop-the-grothendieck-group-of-o-has-simple-and-standard-bases]]) the finite alternating sum of Verma classes equals the class of the simple module:

$$[L(\lambda)]=\sum_{w\in W}(-1)^{\ell(w)}[M(w\circ\lambda)].$$

Equivalently, applying the character homomorphism and the Verma character $\operatorname{ch}M(\mu)=e^{\mu}\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(1-e^{-\alpha})^{-1}$ ([[prop-formal-character-of-a-verma-module]]),

$$\operatorname{ch}L(\lambda)=\sum_{w\in W}(-1)^{\ell(w)}e^{w\circ\lambda}\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(1-e^{-\alpha})^{-1},$$

the Weyl numerator identity in the form needed by the Weyl character formula. Proof: an exact finite complex has vanishing alternating sum of classes.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). For every dominant
integral weight $\lambda\in\Lambda^+$, the character of the finite-dimensional
simple module $L(\lambda)$ is
$$\operatorname{ch}L(\lambda)=A(\lambda+\rho)\cdot A(\rho)^{-1}=\Bigl(\sum_{w\in W}(-1)^{\ell(w)}e^{w(\lambda+\rho)}\Bigr)\Big/\Bigl(e^{\rho}\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(1-e^{-\alpha})\Bigr),$$
the quotient being taken in the completed character ring $\mathcal R$ of
[[def-completed-formal-character-ring-for-downward-cones]], where
$A(\rho)$ is invertible with inverse
$e^{-\rho}\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(1-e^{-\alpha})^{-1}$
([[thm-weyl-denominator-identity]],
[[lem-geometric-series-invertibility-in-the-completed-character-ring]]). No
quotient of ordinary functions is intended before this formal cancellation is
justified.

derivations.claim: **The two matrix products.** Write the displayed matrix as $B$. The product $AB$ has entries $(AB)_{y,w}=\sum_{x:\,y\le x}B_{x,w}$, a sum over the interval $[y,\cdot]$; reading rows $x$ of $B$ against the comparability lists of [F2]: for $y=123$ the six rows of $B$ sum to $(1,0,0,0,0,0)$; for $y=213$ the rows with $x\in\{213,231,312,321\}$ sum to $(0,1,0,0,0,0)$; for $y=132$ the rows with $x\in\{132,231,312,321\}$ sum to $(0,0,1,0,0,0)$; for $y=231$ the rows $231,321$ sum to $(0,0,0,1,0,0)$; for $y=312$ the rows $312,321$ sum to $(0,0,0,0,1,0)$; for $y=321$ the last row is $(0,0,0,0,0,1)$. Hence $AB=I$. Since $A$ is unitriangular by [F2], it has an integral two-sided inverse (the finite geometric series for $I+(A-I)$), so $AB=I$ implies $B=A^{-1}$ and $BA=I$. Equivalently, $(BA)_{y,w}=\sum_{x:\,x\le w}B_{y,x}$ sum over the lower ideal of the column label, rather than over a prefix of the displayed order; for example the row-$123$ sums at $w=132$ and $w=312$ are $1-1=0$ and $1-1-1+1=0$ respectively.

**The inverse coefficients.** By [F3] the matrix of inverse Kazhdan–Lusztig coefficients is $Q'=P^{-1}$, and by [F4] its specialization at $v=1$ is $A^{-1}=B$; hence $q'_{x,w}(1)=B_{x,w}$ for all $x,w$, the entries of $B$ being integers, some negative. Substituting the rows of $B$ into the character formula of [F1], with the support $x\ge w$ of [F2], gives exactly the six displayed identities: row $123$ is $(1,-1,-1,1,1,-1)$, row $213$ is $(0,1,0,-1,-1,1)$ and row $132$ is $(0,0,1,-1,-1,1)$, row $231$ is $(1,0,-1)$ on the labels $231,312,321$, row $312$ is $(1,-1)$ on $312,321$, and row $321$ is $1$.

**The $w=123$ row and the Euler characteristic.** On the labels ordered by [F2], the first row of $B$ is $q'_{123,x}(1)=(-1)^{\ell(x)}$: the values are $+1$ at $x=123$ (length $0$), $-1$ at $x=213,132$ (length $1$), $+1$ at $x=231,312$ (length $2$) and $-1$ at $x=321$ (length $3$). Hence the row-$123$ identity of step 2.1 is $\mathrm{ch}\,L(0)=\sum_{x}(-1)^{\ell(x)}\mathrm{ch}\,M(x\cdot0)$, the BGG Euler-characteristic expression; by [F6] applied to the dominant integral weight $0$ this is the class of $L(0)$ in the Grothendieck group of the block, and by [F7] $\mathrm{ch}\,L(0)=A(\rho)A(\rho)^{-1}=1$ is the character of the trivial module. This independent check confirms the signed inversion: all Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials are $1$, yet the inverse coefficients are signed integers.
